effect_mechanism: The sources point in opposite directions for different kinds of terrace and different kinds of diversity. The WOCAT compiler for contour stone bunds in Bhutan rates plant diversity as greatly increased, linking it to the soil becoming suitable for more diverse crops [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_6891_2023_plant_diversity]. A rangeland-restoration review cites Stavi et al. (2015) from Israel suggesting that earthen contour bench terraces built by heavy machinery, which strip the soil's A-horizon from the hillslope, reduce the species richness of herbaceous vegetation, with Stavi and Argaman (2016) adding that the topsoil removal degrades soil quality [ev_biodiversity_outcome_stav20_9].
conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is how the terrace is built and what is counted: hand-built stone bunds on cropland are credited with more crop diversity, while bulldozed earthen terraces on rangeland are linked to fewer wild herbaceous species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_6891_2023_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_stav20_9]. Neither side is a measured species or habitat comparison: the Bhutan unit is a compiler rating and the Israeli unit a cited suggestion in a review, and neither comes from the target low-income contexts. A measured biodiversity outcome on terraced land, with the construction method stated, is needed before a direction can be given.

effect_mechanism: Carbon removals come from more vegetation and more soil organic matter on treated land. WOCAT compilers attribute storage gains to vegetation: the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso raises biomass production many times over nearby unploughed soil, gabions and rock check dams in Somalia increase biomass and, through vegetation recovery and sediment accumulation, soil organic matter, a haffir in Somalia allows vegetation cover to regenerate, and gradoni orchard terraces in Uzbekistan add below-ground organic matter through expanding roots [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_7778_2026_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7778_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7777_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7553_2025_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. The Somali compiler adds that vegetation recovery and increased biomass store more carbon in plants and soils by absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_7778_2026_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In the literature zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter while trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A check-dam review cites check dams on China's Loess Plateau contributing to carbon sequestration, an effect that grows with time at both dam and watershed level as sediment accumulates [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. The same preprint meta-analysis finds terracing raised soil organic carbon by 27%, 17.94% and 26.62% in three Chinese regions, with increases of 14.11% to 60.96% in regional subsets 11 to 30 years after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_5, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_11]. A Chinese meta-analysis, available as a preprint, reports fish-scale pits raising soil organic carbon storage by 79.86% on the Loess Plateau in years 11~30 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. In Burkina Faso, soils on farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher carbon and nitrogen contents than the control farm [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3], and a review cites climate-smart packages of soil and water conservation structures with biological measures boosting soil carbon stock by three to seven times over business-as-usual [ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3].
conditionality: The WOCAT units are compiler ratings from technology sheets in Burkina Faso, Somalia, Uzbekistan and Bhutan, not measurements, and soil organic matter and emission ratings are proxies rather than measured carbon storage; the Bhutan sheet describes organic matter moving downslope within each terrace, a redistribution rather than a net removal [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_6891_2023_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. The literature is mixed: trenches in Mexico lowered soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso found no significant change in organic matter by the end of the experiment even though biomass rose [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The Loess Plateau check-dam finding is a secondary citation in a review, with no magnitude in the quoted passage [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. The Chinese figures come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country. Several are the values for the duration window with the greatest increase rather than a pooled estimate, and the duration subsets overlap the regional ones [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. The Burkina Faso result is a carbon content on farm soils, not a stock change, and the three-to-sevenfold stock gain is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures, very large for structures and to be read with caution [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

effect_mechanism: Groundwater recharge now counts as a component of catchment water yield, so this row holds two kinds of evidence. Most units report recharge and rising water tables at or near capture structures: the proportion of runoff infiltrated through check dams can reach more than 50%, with recharge linked to episodic storm events [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_luca21_1]; groundwater tables rise in the vicinity of filled check dams, and sand dams can raise the local groundwater [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_fran21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1]; in India additional recharge from check dams and other water harvesting structures was estimated at 480 million cubic meters per annum, groundwater levels rose in 16 of 21 non-desert districts with an average increase of 1.42 meters, and a state survey found levels increased in 22 of the 31 districts [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_3, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_2]; the Uttarakhand water budget shows aquifer recharge up 3.3 percent and water yield from catchment areas up 4.9 percent [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5], and ISRO survey data record increased recharge in treated areas [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3]; terraces would cause a groundwater recharge of 15 to 25% of rainfall, and modelling of contour ridges in Morocco estimates a 50% increase in recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_roose06_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_willem21_1]; stone bunds, zaï and half-moons applied at watershed scale increase ground water level, and in Burkina Faso improved well levels are linked to SWC measures that control surface runoff and improve infiltration [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1]; communities in Mauritania, spate beneficiaries in Yemen and an Ethiopian public-works assessment report rising well levels, increased groundwater or water-table improvements [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_eth16_7]; and a review lists aquifer recharge among benefits cited for water harvesting [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_saru19_1]. Reductions are measured on flow leaving the treated land: On China's Loess Plateau, a large campaign of check-dam construction carried out since the 1970s to retain floodwater and intercept soil sediments reduced streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], and in the Maghreb mechanised bund systems, built with large machines that scrape a 4 to 10 m strip to raise bunds 1.5 to 2 m high every 30 to 50 m, considerably reduce the water collected in downstream hill reservoirs and cost 10 to 25% of the cultivable area [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]. In Burkina Faso, cited studies show soil and water conservation techniques improving the availability of ground water in many villages, especially large rock bunds known as digues filtrantes [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. Embrapa says its barraginhas in Brazil help recharge groundwater by raising the water table and revitalise springs and rivers [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6]. Reviews of Indian studies add recharge figures: about 3–8% of rainfall from well measurements near structures (Badiger et al. 2002), 11% of annual rainfall per structure in Gujarat (Sharda et al. 2006) and around 7% in the Arvari watershed (Glendenning and Vervoort 2010), and an overall 16% increase in recharge across 16 observation wells in Maharashtra, equal to 2% of local annual rainfall (Gore et al. 1998) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_4]; in Ethiopia's Mendae catchment recharge rose from 8 mm before water-harvesting interventions to 107.7 mm after (Negusse et al. 2013) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_gebr18_11]; sand dams in Kenya enhance groundwater recharge (Hut et al. 2008) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_biaz12_27]; and seepage from a Burkina Faso farm pond is described as recharging the groundwater [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8]. The reductions are now more numerous, mostly modelled and mostly Indian: watershed development including more rainwater harvesting was estimated to cut runoff by approximately 60% while raising recharge by only 5% (Sharma and Thakur 2007), rainwater harvesting was suggested to close a basin in Andhra Pradesh so that no more water flowed downstream (Calder et al. 2008), it reduced streamflow in the Arvari model (Glendenning and Vervoort 2011), a global model put the average reduction in annual river flows at 18% with up to 80% in a single basin (Wisser et al. 2010), water outflows from treated catchments were halved against untreated ones (Garg et al. 2012; Gates et al. 2011), and investment in water harvesting upstream is cited as cutting runoff generation for downstream users [ev_water_yield_glen12_2, ev_water_yield_glen12_5, ev_water_yield_glen12_7, ev_water_yield_glen12_10, ev_water_yield_gebr18_9, ev_water_yield_dile13_9].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. The studies found real effects in both directions, and what separates them is where and at what scale they measure. The gains are recharge and well levels at or near the structures; the losses are streamflow, runoff and reservoir inflow below large-scale or basin-wide works — a check-dam campaign built to retain floodwater, mechanised bunds, and Indian watershed development modelled at catchment scale, where the main change in the water balance was more evapotranspiration [ev_water_yield_glen12_2]. Both can hold at once: the Arvari model found rainwater harvesting reduced streamflow while making groundwater more reliable [ev_water_yield_glen12_7], and the global model that cut river flows also raised crop production [ev_water_yield_glen12_10]. Scale matters on the recharge side too: a theoretical model found the impact on water levels minimal beyond the immediate vicinity of a structure (Neumann et al. 2004) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_8], and other catchment studies found intensified small-scale upstream water management had limited or no downstream impact on stream flows (Schreider et al. 2002; De Winnaar and Jewitt 2010; Andersson et al. 2011) [ev_water_yield_dile13_10], as did a water-harvesting review for widely implemented small-scale storage [ev_water_yield_rock10_1]; trenches in the Peruvian Andes had little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics key to explaining their impact [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1]. For a Task Team Leader the practical reading is that dispersed small structures mainly recharge local aquifers, while basin-wide intensification can take water from downstream users and calls for a basin water balance before scaling up. The recharge side has limits in its own sources: the sand-dam effect is often limited in space and time [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1]; in India, pumping from tube wells that land-owning farmers sank as the water table rose has possibly wiped out any increases in recharge from the watershed treatments, and without data from untreated sites the project impact is unclear [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3]; in Burkina Faso the number of wells with water year round has not increased significantly since SWC began [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_2]; and catchment-level recharge gains in the Andes are plausible but cannot be generalised [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1]. Most recharge units are secondary citations, programme reports or modelling, the Mendae figure is a before-and-after water balance cited in a review, and the Burkina Faso pond recharge is inferred from seepage losses rather than measured [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_gebr18_11, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8]. On the loss side, the 39% is a figure the check-dam review cites from another study (Shi et al., 2015) for one Chinese region [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], the Maghreb reduction is a narrative from a Moroccan expert manual with no figure for the water lost downstream, the 10 to 25% being cultivable area rather than water [ev_water_yield_roos10_1], and the Indian reductions are model results cited in reviews, including a basin closure that later reversed as the structures silted up [ev_water_yield_glen12_5]. The digues filtrantes finding is cited from another study, with no figures [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. The barraginha recharge statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measurement behind it [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].

effect_mechanism: Capturing runoff upstream moves water from the stream into the ground. On the recharge side, works that hold water on the land let it infiltrate and raise local water tables: in Maharashtra a groundwater model of 16 observation wells found an overall increase in recharge from rainwater harvesting of 16% (Gore et al., 1998, cited by Glendenning et al.), well measurements near structures put recharge at about 3–8% of rainfall (Badiger et al., 2002), and in Ethiopia's Mendae catchment a water balance gave groundwater recharge of 107.7 mm after water harvesting against 8 mm before (Negusse et al., 2013, cited by Gebremeskel et al.) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_gebr18_11]. Terraces in the Mandara mountains are reported to recharge the water table by 15 to 25% of rainfall (Hiol Hiol and Mietton, cited by Roose), modelling of contour ridges in Morocco estimates a 50% rise in recharge (cited by Willems et al.), and check dams and other structures in Saurashtra were estimated to add 480 million cubic meters of recharge per annum (Jain, 2012, cited by Verma and Shah) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_roose06_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_willem21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_1]. In Rajasthan piezometers recorded groundwater rising in 16 of 21 non-desert districts by an average of 1.42 meters, and after tank desilting in Telangana a state survey found levels up in 22 of the 31 districts [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_3, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_2]; a water budget for Uttarakhand's watershed project put aquifer recharge 3.3 percent above baseline [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5]. Rising well levels are also reported around stone bunds, zaï and half-moons in Burkina Faso, earth and stone bunds in Mauritania, spate and conservation structures in Yemen, filled check dams (Frankl et al., 2016; Lucas-Borja et al., 2018), sand dams (Hut et al., 2008), and Ethiopian public-works watersheds where a better water table allowed small-scale irrigation [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_fran21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_biaz12_27, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_eth16_7], and a Burkina Faso farm-pond study treats seepage from the reservoir as recharge rather than lost water [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8]. On the outflow side, the same capture reduces the water that leaves the catchment: a GIS and water-balance study estimated that watershed development including more rainwater harvesting would cut runoff by approximately 60% while raising recharge by only 5% (Sharma and Thakur, 2007), a global model suggested rainwater harvesting would reduce annual river flows by 18% on average and by up to 80% in a single basin (Wisser et al., 2010), and in Andhra Pradesh it was suggested to cause basin closure (Calder et al., 2008), all cited by Glendenning et al. [ev_water_yield_glen12_2, ev_water_yield_glen12_10, ev_water_yield_glen12_5]. Outflows from treated catchments have been found halved compared with untreated ones (Garg et al., 2012; Gates et al., 2011, cited by Gebremeskel et al.), reviews cite decreased runoff generation harming downstream systems, a Rajasthan model found rainwater harvesting reducing streamflow, and in Morocco mechanised bunds considerably reduce the water collected in downstream hill reservoirs (Albergel et al., 2004, cited by Roose et al.) [ev_water_yield_gebr18_9, ev_water_yield_dile13_9, ev_water_yield_glen12_7, ev_water_yield_roos10_1].
conditionality: Studies disagree on the direction because they measure different water. The recharge side counts water entering the ground near the works; the outflow side counts water leaving the catchment for downstream users, and the same capture can raise the first while lowering the second, as in the watershed where runoff fell by about 60% and recharge rose by only 5%, with most of the change going to evapotranspiration [ev_water_yield_glen12_2]. Scale and intensity separate them too: several studies find limited or no downstream impact from small-scale water storage even when implemented widely (Evenari et al., 1971; Schreider et al., 2002; Sreedevi et al., 2006; De Winnaar and Jewitt, 2010; Andersson et al., 2011) [ev_water_yield_rock10_1, ev_water_yield_dile13_10], a theoretical model found the effect on water levels minimal beyond the immediate vicinity of a structure (Neumann et al., 2004) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_8], while the large flow reductions come from intensive watershed development, basin-wide models and mechanised bunds. Siltation of the structures can also reverse basin closure by letting downstream flows rise again [ev_water_yield_glen12_5]. The recharge gains are not secure: in Burkina Faso a reconnaissance of 59 villages found that the number of wells with water year-round had not increased significantly since soil and water conservation began [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_2]; in India the survey data showed more recharge in treated areas but had no untreated sites, and tube-well pumping encouraged by subsidised electricity has possibly wiped out the gains [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_4]. Most units on both sides are second-hand citations, models or self-reported project results (the Uttarakhand, Mauritania and Yemen figures come from World Bank completion reports), and few measure both recharge and downstream flow in the same catchment. This row is for downstream users and basin planners; spring and stream discharge gains near treated watersheds are local supply and are reported in the water stress rows, not here.

effect_mechanism: Storage structures recharge groundwater around them. Check dams can infiltrate more than 50% of runoff, with recharge linked to episodic storm events, and groundwater tables rise near filled check dams [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_luca21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_fran21_1]. Sand dams can raise the local groundwater, and Biazin et al. cite Hut et al. (2008) for sand dams in Kenya enhancing groundwater recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_biaz12_27]. In India additional recharge from check dams and other water harvesting structures was estimated at 480 million cubic meters per annum, and a state survey found groundwater levels increased in 22 of the 31 districts [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_2]. An Indian review cites Badiger et al. (2002) inferring recharge of about 3–8% of rainfall near structures and Sharda et al. (2006) estimating that 11% of annual rainfall could recharge from a structure, and Gore et al. (1998) modelling an overall 16% increase in groundwater recharge from rainwater harvesting in Maharashtra [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_4]. A farm-pond study in Burkina Faso treats seepage as groundwater recharge, a review lists aquifer recharge among cited benefits, and Embrapa says its barraginhas raise the water table and revitalise springs [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_saru19_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].
conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is where the water is counted. Recharge is measured or modelled at or near the structures, while the harm side is flow leaving the watershed: on China's Loess Plateau the check-dam campaign reduced streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], and the Indian review cites Sharma and Thakur (2007) estimating that watershed development including more rainwater harvesting would cut runoff by approximately 60% while raising recharge by only 5%, mostly through more evapotranspiration from irrigation, Calder et al. (2008) suggesting rainwater harvesting could close a basin in Andhra Pradesh so no water flows further downstream, and Glendenning and Vervoort (2011) modelling reduced streamflow in Rajasthan [ev_water_yield_glen12_2, ev_water_yield_glen12_5, ev_water_yield_glen12_7]. A theoretical study cited there, Neumann et al. (2004), found the effect on watershed water levels may be minimal beyond the immediate vicinity of a structure, and the sand-dam effect is often limited in space and time [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_8, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1]. So local recharge gains for wells near the works can coexist with less water for downstream users and basin planners. Almost every unit is a secondary citation, an estimate or a model; the Burkina Faso recharge is the authors' inference from seepage, and the barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_foxr03_8, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].

In a Kenyan catchment with sand dams the number of people exposed to droughts fell from 420 to 0 while a control catchment stayed at 600 [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In Ethiopia, the Sustainable Land Management Programme reduced vulnerability to severe drought in treated watersheds against control watersheds, with programme effects three times larger where severe droughts occurred, and buffered moderate droughts significantly on both vegetation measures used [ev_drought_hazard_cons22_1, ev_drought_hazard_cons22_2]. effect_mechanism: Ponds, cisterns and check dams store runoff for use in dry periods: pond water used as supplemental irrigation reduces crop-loss risk in irregular years in semi-arid Brazil, cisterns in China are reported to be mitigating frequent periods of drought, a review of small reservoirs counts improved drought resilience among their cited benefits, and the compiler of a Cambodian on-farm pond sheet states the pond provides enough water even during drought [ev_drought_hazard_brito07_10, ev_drought_hazard_iegchn07_4, ev_drought_hazard_saru19_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_2844_2017_drought_impacts]. The WOCAT compiler for gabions and rock check dams in Somalia likewise judges drought impacts reduced, citing improved soil moisture retention and water infiltration [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_drought_impacts]. In a Kenyan catchment with sand dams the number of people exposed to droughts fell from 420 to 0 while a control catchment stayed at 600 [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. In Brazil, Embrapa describes its barraginhas, small semicircular runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in pastures and croplands, as storing water in the soil by infiltration and easing the effects of droughts on crops in the lowlands [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. A Burkina Faso risk analysis of a farm reservoir used for supplemental irrigation finds that all of the mild dry spells can be mitigated, which explains the more frequent zero-stress seasons under irrigation than in the control, and that severe dry spells late in the season are partly mitigated, turned into mild ones [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_7, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. A conceptual watershed model for the Arvari watershed in Rajasthan showed rainwater harvesting gave a slight buffer in drought years through more reliable groundwater stores (Glendenning and Vervoort, 2011, cited by Glendenning et al.) [ev_drought_hazard_glen12_6].
conditionality: The class is held at moderate because few of the benefit units say how big the effect is. Most of the pool is practitioner judgements and assertions without drought-loss metrics: an expert account from Brazil, a lender evaluation in China, compiler ratings from Cambodia and Somalia, and a review that counts how often small-reservoir studies cite improved drought resilience; only a Kenyan sand-dam catchment table compares people exposed to droughts against a control catchment, and its values are likely interview-derived [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. Subsurface dams in Brazil tended to dry out in a rainless year and small ones do not withstand long dry spells, which records no benefit when storage is exhausted rather than damage to the works [ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_2, ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_3]. The barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measured drought contrast and no normal-year reference [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8]. The Burkina Faso analysis marks the limit of storage: a drought year, with a probability of 0.1, cannot be mitigated because there is insufficient water to harvest, and the late severe dry spells need at least three irrigation applications while the reservoir supports only two [ev_drought_hazard_fox05_5, ev_drought_hazard_fox05_6]. The Rajasthan buffer is a model result cited second-hand, and the same model showed rainwater harvesting reducing streamflow [ev_drought_hazard_glen12_6].

effect_mechanism: Terraces, contour stone bunds, check dams and small dams slow and spread runoff and retain water and sediment, lowering peak discharges: terraces lowered flood peaks on small mountain plots, stone bunds lower peak discharges at the foot of the slope, and in a semi-arid Tunisian catchment a combined treatment cut the runoff volume of 71 single-peak floods by 50% [ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose06_2_s]. WOCAT compilers in Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, Tunisia and Uzbekistan rate flooding as reduced and say how: rain retained where it falls, a dam or series of dams acting as a downstream buffer, stone lines and walls cutting peak flows, and structures slowing runoff velocity [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1537_2012_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6610_2022_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6715_2023_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_6716_2023_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7553_2025_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_7778_2026_flood_impacts]. Users of small reservoirs in Ghana perceive fewer rainy-season floods, spate and diversion structures in Yemen are said to control floods, and compacted hill terraces in Uttarakhand, India are credited with limiting flood and landslide damage [ev_flood_hazard_veno12_1, ev_flood_hazard_yem12_4, ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7]. A check-dam review cites check dams mitigating flooding and significantly reducing peak flow in Iran and check-dam sequences proving effective against strong floods in Italian torrents, and small hill dams in Morocco are credited with damping damage in the serious 2002-2003 floods [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2, ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1]. Embrapa credits its barraginhas, small runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in Brazil, with easing floods as well [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].
conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, and the split runs through terracing: bunds and terraces that slow and spread runoff on the slope lowered peak discharges, while structures that divert runoff did the opposite — diversion banquettes in Niger raised peak discharges and runoff-diversion systems accelerate concentration time [ev_flood_hazard_roose94_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose06_1, ev_flood_hazard_heusch95_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose94_3]. Runoff-catchment and spate rows each show a moderate benefit on their own, so whether the practice eases or worsens flood hazard depends on whether it holds water in place or concentrates it. Size and extremes matter too: larger sand dams increase flooding risk, and check dams have a minimal effect against extreme floods, especially where ill-designed or poorly maintained [ev_flood_hazard_ritc21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3]. Catchment-scale measurement is scarce, with a review calling the terrace effect on peak flow uncertain; the Tunisian result bundles rangeland closure and gully stone-filling with the bunds, the Yemen and Uttarakhand statements are lender self-reported, the review's supporting cases are secondary citations, and the Italian ones are mountain torrent control in a high-income setting [ev_flood_hazard_willem21_1, ev_flood_hazard_roose06_2_s, ev_flood_hazard_yem12_4, ev_flood_hazard_utk22_7, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2]. The barraginha flood statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, unmeasured, and a landscape-scale effect rather than one on the adopting farm [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].

effect_mechanism: Water harvesting and soil and water conservation reduce food insecurity mainly by raising and steadying harvests and by putting stored water on gardens. In the Brazilian semi-arid, subsurface dams gave families more fruit and vegetables and, by most interviewees' account, more food overall, and production cisterns allow daily irrigation of gardens in households that had not grown or eaten vegetables before [ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_arsky20_6]; in Burkina Faso, runoff cisterns irrigate small gardens and water livestock, improving food security in the lean season [ev_food_security_roose94_1]. In the field, planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a Kenyan plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, and ground cover raised those odds in Malawi's El Nino season [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Household food security rises in proportion to the area of a farm improved with bunds, and beneficiaries of Rwanda's terracing project showed drastically improved food consumption scores against a comparison group [ev_food_security_zoug14_1, ev_food_security_rwa18_5]. WOCAT compilers rate food self-sufficiency as improved and the risk of production failure as lowered, and say why: enough stored water to irrigate during drought in Cambodia, better soil moisture in Ethiopia, more cultivable land and crop diversity in Bhutan, more productive fodder and crops in Burkina Faso, and rehabilitated gullies and farmland in Somalia [ev_food_security_wocat_2844_2017_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_6715_2023_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_6891_2023_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_6891_2023_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_7778_2026_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Ethiopia's Anjene catchment, farmers recalled that before terracing the community was highly food insecure and migrated in search of food even in minor droughts, and that terraces improved crop production and reduced seasonal migration [ev_food_security_adgo13_11]. Ethiopian farmers who adopted rainwater-harvesting irrigation properly improved their dietary status (Desta 2004, cited in a review) [ev_food_security_biaz12_26].
conditionality: The gains depend on the rainfall year, on where the works are built and on practice choice. In Niger, farm families with soil and water conservation produced an estimated surplus of 70 percent in good rainfall years but a deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]; in Malawi's El Nino season, banking lowered the odds of meeting the maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. Independent evaluations of Ethiopian programmes found communal, mostly off-farm watershed works did not raise food security, possibly because the programmes were short [ev_food_security_abate21_4, ev_food_security_arega24_1], and compilers record no change for vetiver terraces in Haiti, where land users must wait for degraded soil to recover [ev_food_security_wocat_3223_2017_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Much of the literature is cited second-hand or qualitative, and the Brazilian findings include Embrapa's assessment of its own technology and programme reviews [ev_food_security_mira19_2, ev_food_security_castro22_3]. The class is moderate because the sub-practices differ, from slight for cross-family evidence to strong for in-field practices. A gain in a good season does not by itself show the practice protects food supply through drought. The Anjene account rests on farmer recall and group discussions, and the dietary finding is second-hand with no magnitude [ev_food_security_adgo13_11, ev_food_security_biaz12_26].

effect_mechanism: Harvested water and held soil moisture raise harvests and diversify diets: in semi-arid Kenya planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, bunds improve household food security in proportion to the farm area they cover, and Burkina Faso farms applying manure or soil and water conservation techniques on over half their plots are cited as more food secure [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_zoug14_1, ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5]. In semi-arid Brazil stored production water allows daily irrigation of vegetable gardens and fruit trees for families who previously did not grow or eat vegetables, subsurface dams gave families more access to fruit and vegetables and more food overall, reviews of production-cistern experiments stress their importance for food security, and a systematic review cites significant improvements in food security indicators among adopters of rainwater-harvesting ponds in Burkina Faso [ev_food_security_arsky20_6, ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_castro22_3, ev_food_security_silv26_1].
conditionality: The gain depends on rain: Niger farm families with soil and water conservation produced an estimated surplus of 70 percent in years of good rainfall but still had an estimated deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years, so the practice does not secure food in dry years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]. The only sized result is the Kenyan odds ratio, which has a wide confidence interval and comes from an above-average rainfall season [ev_food_security_boil19_2]. The Brazilian units are implementer perceptions, a seven-family interview study and a review of experiments run by the technology's developer, the Burkina Faso farm statement bundles manure with the conservation works, and the systematic review's citation is contradicted by its own table [ev_food_security_arsky20_6, ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_castro22_3, ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5, ev_food_security_silv26_1].

justification.mechanism: Harvested water and held soil moisture raise harvests and diversify diets: in semi-arid Kenya planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, bunds improve household food security in proportion to the farm area they cover, and Burkina Faso farms applying manure or soil and water conservation techniques on over half their plots are cited as more food secure [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_zoug14_1, ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5]. In semi-arid Brazil stored production water allows daily irrigation of vegetable gardens and fruit trees for families who previously did not grow or eat vegetables, subsurface dams gave families more access to fruit and vegetables and more food overall, reviews of production-cistern experiments stress their importance for food security, and a systematic review cites significant improvements in food security indicators among adopters of rainwater-harvesting ponds in Burkina Faso [ev_food_security_arsky20_6, ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_castro22_3, ev_food_security_silv26_1].
justification.conditionality: The gain depends on rain: Niger farm families with soil and water conservation produced an estimated surplus of 70 percent in years of good rainfall but still had an estimated deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years, so the practice does not secure food in dry years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]. The only sized result is the Kenyan odds ratio, which has a wide confidence interval and comes from an above-average rainfall season [ev_food_security_boil19_2]. The Brazilian units are implementer perceptions, a seven-family interview study and a review of experiments run by the technology's developer, the Burkina Faso farm statement bundles manure with the conservation works, and the systematic review's citation is contradicted by its own table [ev_food_security_arsky20_6, ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_castro22_3, ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5, ev_food_security_silv26_1].

effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income semi-arid Brazil, stored water lets families grow food close to home: once production water is stored it allows daily irrigation of gardens, beds and fruit trees, and most families had not even been in the habit of growing and eating vegetables before [ev_food_security_arsky20_6]. Families with subsurface dams gained more varied diets, mainly through more access to fruit and vegetables, and most of those interviewed reported more food available [ev_food_security_cirilo03_6]; a review of Embrapa experiments judges irrigation of small beds from production cisterns important for household food security [ev_food_security_castro22_3], and adopters of barraginha runoff basins identified food security, in quantity, quality and diversity, as the technology's greatest impact [ev_food_security_mira19_2].
conditionality: The gain is rated slight because no unit gives a size of effect: the evidence is qualitative interviews, an expert account of a cistern programme, a review of the research institute's own experiments, and an adopter-rated indicator in Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology [ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_food_security_arsky20_6, ev_food_security_castro22_3, ev_food_security_mira19_2]. All of it comes from semi-arid Brazil and works through garden irrigation and diet diversity rather than staple-crop supply, so it describes household storage for home production, not field-scale harvesting.

effect_mechanism: Works that raise and steady crop output reduce the times a household runs short of food. In Ethiopia's Anjene catchment, which two decades earlier was highly eroded and highly food insecure, with people migrating in search of food in times of even minor droughts, the introduction of fanya juu terraces improved crop production and so reduced seasonal migration of farmers [ev_food_security_adgo13_11]. In Brazil, adopters of Embrapa's barraginhas, small semicircular runoff-retention basins, identified food security as the technology's greatest impact, because it guarantees quantity, quality and diversity of food [ev_food_security_mira19_2].
conditionality: Both units say food security improved but neither says by how much: the Ethiopian finding rests on farmer recall and group discussions about the period before and after terracing, and the terraces were maintained for decades with community labour alongside fertiliser use on cereals [ev_food_security_adgo13_11]. The Brazilian finding is an adopter rating in Embrapa's own impact assessment of its technology, not a measured food-security indicator [ev_food_security_mira19_2]. A measured household food-security comparison with untreated farms is needed to state a size.

effect_mechanism: Across mixed soil and water conservation and water-harvesting programmes, the reported route to lower food insecurity is higher yields and irrigated gardens. A review tabulates significantly increased food security from check dams and infiltration pits in Malawi [ev_food_security_ngur26_1]; Brazilian studies judge production-cistern irrigation of small beds feasible and important for household food security [ev_food_security_castro22_3]; and higher yields are cited as improving food security in Burkina Faso, especially on farms with soil and water conservation on over half of their plots [ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5].
conditionality: The gain is only slight because the supporting findings are qualitative, cited second-hand and give no size, while the independent evaluations point the other way. In Ethiopia, an impact evaluation of a bundled watershed project found no significant food-security effect for treated households at any participation level [ev_food_security_abate21_4], and public-works participation in communal soil and water investments did not translate into increased food security, possibly because of the short programme [ev_food_security_arega24_1]; both concern mostly off-farm community works. In Niger, families with soil and water conservation produced a surplus of 70 percent in good rainfall years but a deficit of 28 percent in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1], so benefits may not hold in the dry years that matter most.

The Anjene account rests on farmer recall and group discussions rather than a measured comparison [ev_food_security_adgo13_11].

effect_mechanism: Water harvesting and conservation structures capture runoff and raise soil moisture so rainfed crops yield more, especially in dry years and low-rainfall areas; stored water allows supplemental irrigation and extra crops, and sediment and organic matter trapped behind structures add fertility. Meta-analyses now carry much of the evidence: A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching, 69% for soil and stone bunds, 48% for terraces and 74% for tied ridging [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1], and 2 to 4-year old bench terraces in Peru gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In Burkina Faso stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% and by about 142% with compost, on-farm trials in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare on planting basins and direct-seeded plots, in Malawi's El Niño season ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Stored water stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, sand dams cut crop failure against a control catchment in Kenya, and WOCAT compilers across many technology sheets judge crop, fodder and animal production increased [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials point the same way: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1], and in the same trial runoff from the terrace waterways, collected in a dug, lined pond and applied by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation, gave 11982 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds and by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1, ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï and 1-m half-moons with compost gave 408 and 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1, ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1] and a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. Primary studies acquired in the latest round add to this. A meta-analysis of water-harvesting studies across semi-arid Africa and Asia finds that water harvesting increases crop yields by 78% on average, with a large spread, and puts the average maize gain at almost 3000 kg/ha in Asia against 400 kg/ha in Africa [ev_crop_yield_boum16_1, ev_crop_yield_boum16_5, ev_crop_yield_boum16_6]. Stored runoff used for supplemental irrigation raises yields where rain is short: in Burkina Faso a farm pond lifted the 3-year mean sorghum yield from 455 kg per hectare under the farmer's normal practice to 712 with irrigation alone and 1403 with fertiliser as well [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_1, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_2], and a risk analysis puts the long-term average gain at 150% [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]; in Kenya irrigation from a runoff dam with fertilizer gave 1796 kg of maize per hectare against 1375 on fertilised non-irrigated plots [ev_crop_yield_barr05_1]; and in Pakistan supplemental irrigation from harvested rainwater raised wheat yield by 146%, mustard by 101%, maize by 118% and pearl millet by 101% over rainfed fields [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_2, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_3, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_4]. In-field works raise yields by holding rain where it falls: terraced fields in Ethiopia's Anjene catchment gave 0.95, 1.86 and 1.73 t of teff, barley and maize per hectare against 0.49, 0.61 and 0.77 t on un-terraced farms [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3]; in Nigeria tied ridging raised four-year mean sorghum yield by 25% and tied ridging with mulch by 57% [ev_crop_yield_chir06_1, ev_crop_yield_chir06_3]; Zambian basins averaged 4.4 t of maize per hectare against 1.7 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar12_1], and in Malawi conservation agriculture (planting in small holes under residue cover) gave 600 kg per hectare more grain than conventional ridge tillage in 2016/17 [ev_crop_yield_seti18_2]. Plot-level econometrics in Ethiopia agree for drier areas: conserved plots in low-rainfall Tigray carry a yield premium of ETB 412 or 299 per hectare depending on the estimator, and all the soil and water conservation technologies studied had robust impacts on crop output in low-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_1]. Output also steadies: in Kenya the coefficient of variation of maize yield was 5% with irrigation and fertilizer against 11% in the control, Nigerian sorghum under tied ridging with mulch fell below 1000 kg per hectare once in four years against three times on the flat bed, and in Malawi yield variation was lower under conservation agriculture [ev_yield_stability_barr05_8, ev_yield_stability_chir06_12, ev_yield_stability_seti18_3]. Reviews add second-hand gains: tied ridges improving barley grain yield by at least 44% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), stone rows or grass strips raising sorghum yield by 12–58% in Burkina Faso (Zougmore et al., 2004), basin tillage with mulching raising maize yields by 30–50% on a South African clay (Hensley et al., 2000; Walker et al., 2005), soil bunds giving at least 30% more lowland rice in Tanzania in normal years (Raes et al., 2007), and stone bunds and terraces raising crop yield by up to 53% in Ethiopia (Nyssen et al., 2007) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_9, ev_crop_yield_dile13_3, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_23, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_12, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_16, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_2].
conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: where rainfall is heavy the practice can lower yields through waterlogging, and the authors say so. Annual rainfall above 1000 mm lowered the performance of Ethiopian soil and water conservation practices, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, and fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]; in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: the practice should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. Other measured losses do count against the class: bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years in Ethiopia, and stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. The sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds no significant gain for crops other than maize, and outperformance of conventional tillage only with no-tillage systems rather than planting basins or minimum tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_3, ev_crop_yield_corb20_9]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture consistently underperforms on high-clay soils in very wet seasons, though at median rainfall and clay it outperforms conventional practice even without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_stew18_3, ev_crop_yield_stew18_4]; and in drought seasons in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. In Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. Other nulls and negatives: conservation promoted mostly off-farm had no yield effect, benefits in Ethiopia appeared only once structures were maintained for at least seven years, diversion banquettes in Niger cut yields, and soil salinisation can appear on check-dam farmland [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Outside the meta-analyses the pool mixes independent evaluations with lender completion-report figures, bundled watershed programmes, reviews quoting ranges from earlier studies, a farmer survey reported in a preprint and many practitioner judgements; much of the zai and planting-basin gain rides on added manure, compost or fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Burkina Faso farm gains are for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; and the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO cross-slope barrier mark is a compiler judgement, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. The newer primaries also mark where the gain stops. Supplemental irrigation pays mainly in dry seasons and with fertiliser: in Kenya it left yield unchanged or slightly lower in good rainfall seasons (>350 mm), and irrigation alone did not increase grain yield [ev_crop_yield_barr05_7, ev_crop_yield_barr05_2]; in Burkina Faso irrigated and non-irrigated plots did not differ significantly at the same fertiliser level, so fertiliser was the main reason for the higher yields, and the gain from irrigation alone does not cover the heavy investment of labour and capital [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_3, ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. In Ethiopia's high-rainfall Amhara, conserved plots showed no significant yield difference, the point estimate lying ETB 179 or 145 per hectare below non-conserved plots, and only waterways and trees had robust impacts in high-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_2]; soil bunds raised production risk in Tigray, the driest region studied, and irrigation alone did so too unless combined with improved seed and fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_kato11_6, ev_yield_stability_kato11_8]. Nigerian ridging without mulch yielded 9 and 3% less than the flat bed in 2000, when rain failed at flowering and grain filling [ev_crop_yield_chir06_5]; in Ghana tied ridges made no significant difference to maize yield [ev_crop_yield_dalt14_1]; in Mozambique basin and direct-seeded maize yields did not differ [ev_crop_yield_kida19_1]; and in the meta-analysis most of the 21 observations with a lower yield were in-soil storage techniques [ev_crop_yield_boum16_2]. Rodents sheltering in narrowly spaced stone bunds can damage up to 225 kg of crop per hectare (Meheretu et al., 2014) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_4]. The larger Nigerian gain comes with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_3], and the meta-analysis's Asian maize gain far exceeds the African average [ev_crop_yield_boum16_6], so the size of the gain depends heavily on the package and the region.
