justification.mechanism: Water harvesting and conservation structures capture runoff and raise soil moisture so rainfed crops yield more, especially in dry years and low-rainfall areas; stored water allows supplemental irrigation and extra crops, and sediment and organic matter trapped behind structures add fertility. Meta-analyses now carry much of the evidence: A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching, 69% for soil and stone bunds, 48% for terraces and 74% for tied ridging [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1], and 2 to 4-year old bench terraces in Peru gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In Burkina Faso stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% and by about 142% with compost, on-farm trials in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare on planting basins and direct-seeded plots, in Malawi's El Niño season ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Stored water stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, sand dams cut crop failure against a control catchment in Kenya, and WOCAT compilers across many technology sheets judge crop, fodder and animal production increased [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials point the same way: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1], and in the same trial runoff from the terrace waterways, collected in a dug, lined pond and applied by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation, gave 11982 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds and by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1, ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï and 1-m half-moons with compost gave 408 and 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1, ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1] and a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. Primary studies acquired in the latest round add to this. A meta-analysis of water-harvesting studies across semi-arid Africa and Asia finds that water harvesting increases crop yields by 78% on average, with a large spread, and puts the average maize gain at almost 3000 kg/ha in Asia against 400 kg/ha in Africa [ev_crop_yield_boum16_1, ev_crop_yield_boum16_5, ev_crop_yield_boum16_6]. Stored runoff used for supplemental irrigation raises yields where rain is short: in Burkina Faso a farm pond lifted the 3-year mean sorghum yield from 455 kg per hectare under the farmer's normal practice to 712 with irrigation alone and 1403 with fertiliser as well [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_1, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_2], and a risk analysis puts the long-term average gain at 150% [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]; in Kenya irrigation from a runoff dam with fertilizer gave 1796 kg of maize per hectare against 1375 on fertilised non-irrigated plots [ev_crop_yield_barr05_1]; and in Pakistan supplemental irrigation from harvested rainwater raised wheat yield by 146%, mustard by 101%, maize by 118% and pearl millet by 101% over rainfed fields [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_2, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_3, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_4]. In-field works raise yields by holding rain where it falls: terraced fields in Ethiopia's Anjene catchment gave 0.95, 1.86 and 1.73 t of teff, barley and maize per hectare against 0.49, 0.61 and 0.77 t on un-terraced farms [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3]; in Nigeria tied ridging raised four-year mean sorghum yield by 25% and tied ridging with mulch by 57% [ev_crop_yield_chir06_1, ev_crop_yield_chir06_3]; Zambian basins averaged 4.4 t of maize per hectare against 1.7 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar12_1], and in Malawi conservation agriculture (planting in small holes under residue cover) gave 600 kg per hectare more grain than conventional ridge tillage in 2016/17 [ev_crop_yield_seti18_2]. Plot-level econometrics in Ethiopia agree for drier areas: conserved plots in low-rainfall Tigray carry a yield premium of ETB 412 or 299 per hectare depending on the estimator, and all the soil and water conservation technologies studied had robust impacts on crop output in low-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_1]. Output also steadies: in Kenya the coefficient of variation of maize yield was 5% with irrigation and fertilizer against 11% in the control, Nigerian sorghum under tied ridging with mulch fell below 1000 kg per hectare once in four years against three times on the flat bed, and in Malawi yield variation was lower under conservation agriculture [ev_yield_stability_barr05_8, ev_yield_stability_chir06_12, ev_yield_stability_seti18_3]. Reviews add second-hand gains: tied ridges improving barley grain yield by at least 44% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), stone rows or grass strips raising sorghum yield by 12–58% in Burkina Faso (Zougmore et al., 2004), basin tillage with mulching raising maize yields by 30–50% on a South African clay (Hensley et al., 2000; Walker et al., 2005), soil bunds giving at least 30% more lowland rice in Tanzania in normal years (Raes et al., 2007), and stone bunds and terraces raising crop yield by up to 53% in Ethiopia (Nyssen et al., 2007) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_9, ev_crop_yield_dile13_3, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_23, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_12, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_16, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_2].
justification.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: where rainfall is heavy the practice can lower yields through waterlogging, and the authors say so. Annual rainfall above 1000 mm lowered the performance of Ethiopian soil and water conservation practices, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, and fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]; in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: the practice should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. Other measured losses do count against the class: bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years in Ethiopia, and stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. The sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds no significant gain for crops other than maize, and outperformance of conventional tillage only with no-tillage systems rather than planting basins or minimum tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_3, ev_crop_yield_corb20_9]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture consistently underperforms on high-clay soils in very wet seasons, though at median rainfall and clay it outperforms conventional practice even without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_stew18_3, ev_crop_yield_stew18_4]; and in drought seasons in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. In Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. Other nulls and negatives: conservation promoted mostly off-farm had no yield effect, benefits in Ethiopia appeared only once structures were maintained for at least seven years, diversion banquettes in Niger cut yields, and soil salinisation can appear on check-dam farmland [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Outside the meta-analyses the pool mixes independent evaluations with lender completion-report figures, bundled watershed programmes, reviews quoting ranges from earlier studies, a farmer survey reported in a preprint and many practitioner judgements; much of the zai and planting-basin gain rides on added manure, compost or fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Burkina Faso farm gains are for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; and the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO cross-slope barrier mark is a compiler judgement, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. The newer primaries also mark where the gain stops. Supplemental irrigation pays mainly in dry seasons and with fertiliser: in Kenya it left yield unchanged or slightly lower in good rainfall seasons (>350 mm), and irrigation alone did not increase grain yield [ev_crop_yield_barr05_7, ev_crop_yield_barr05_2]; in Burkina Faso irrigated and non-irrigated plots did not differ significantly at the same fertiliser level, so fertiliser was the main reason for the higher yields, and the gain from irrigation alone does not cover the heavy investment of labour and capital [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_3, ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. In Ethiopia's high-rainfall Amhara, conserved plots showed no significant yield difference, the point estimate lying ETB 179 or 145 per hectare below non-conserved plots, and only waterways and trees had robust impacts in high-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_2]; soil bunds raised production risk in Tigray, the driest region studied, and irrigation alone did so too unless combined with improved seed and fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_kato11_6, ev_yield_stability_kato11_8]. Nigerian ridging without mulch yielded 9 and 3% less than the flat bed in 2000, when rain failed at flowering and grain filling [ev_crop_yield_chir06_5]; in Ghana tied ridges made no significant difference to maize yield [ev_crop_yield_dalt14_1]; in Mozambique basin and direct-seeded maize yields did not differ [ev_crop_yield_kida19_1]; and in the meta-analysis most of the 21 observations with a lower yield were in-soil storage techniques [ev_crop_yield_boum16_2]. Rodents sheltering in narrowly spaced stone bunds can damage up to 225 kg of crop per hectare (Meheretu et al., 2014) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_4]. The larger Nigerian gain comes with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_3], and the meta-analysis's Asian maize gain far exceeds the African average [ev_crop_yield_boum16_6], so the size of the gain depends heavily on the package and the region.

effect_mechanism: In the tropical highlands, soil and water conservation has measured yield gains and measured yield losses, depending on the practice. Gains: an Ethiopian synthesis finds mean grain-yield gains of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching, stone and soil bunds raising yields by up to 10% in Tigray, and stone bunds raising soil total nitrogen from 0.16 to 0.20% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4, ev_crop_yield_adim16_8, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1]; in a Kenyan highland trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 4.10 against 3.15 t of maize per hectare with manure and fertiliser, and 2.53 against 1.82 t without inputs (not significant), and tended to give less variable yields [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1]; in Peru, 2 to 4-year old bench terraces gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In the Ethiopian highlands, fields with long-established fanya juu terraces and grass strips yielded 0.95 against 0.49 t of teff, 1.86 against 0.61 t of barley and 1.73 against 0.77 t of maize per hectare on adjacent un-terraced farms, and the terraces improved the water productivity of the three crops by at least 100% [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]. Losses: in the same Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the authors suggest may be waterlogging in the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6].
conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The fanya juu and soil bund losses and the finding that annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively are held out of it, because the synthesis puts that effect down to excessive water availability (water logging) on the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]: they are logged as a performance caveat — these structures should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy — rather than as production evidence. The evidence points to three things that separate gains from losses. Practice type: stone bunds, tied ridges and mulching gained, while graded and level fanya juu, soil bunds and grass strips lost yield in the Ethiopian table [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Rainfall: the gaining practices were studied at lower average rainfall (695.1 mm for tied ridges, 876.7 mm for mulching) than the losing bunds (1030.2 to 1454.3 mm), and rainfall above 1000 mm reduced performance [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; practice and rainfall travel together in that table, so the two cannot be fully separated. Time: bunds lose yield in the first few years, while the long-established fanya juu terraces of the Ethiopian with-and-without survey yielded more than un-terraced fields, so fanya juu is not a losing practice everywhere [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1]. Against those terrace gains, the same paper cites Herweg and Ludi (1999) and Kassie et al. (2008) finding that fanya juu, soil and stone bunds and grass strips did not increase crop yield or biomass in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_12]. For a Task Team Leader the actionable reading is to match the structure to the rainfall regime, favouring in-field moisture capture in drier highlands and avoiding fanya juu and soil bunds where waterlogging is likely, and to budget for an early yield dip. At the dry end, tied ridging gave no advantage in the Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, since there was little rain to hold [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5]. On quality, both sides rest mainly on the same Ethiopian synthesis of unweighted means pooled across studies; the Kenyan result is a single-site trial whose lower-variability finding was not tested, the Peruvian figure is cited in a review, and the Ethiopian terrace gains are descriptive statistics from a comparison of terraced and adjacent un-terraced farms, not a controlled trial [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2].

effect_mechanism: Soil and water conservation and water harvesting have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains come from retaining moisture and soil: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 69% for soil and stone bunds and gains of 71.7% for maize and 68.2% for sorghum without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_7, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_8]; four studies in a systematic review find 20–24 per cent gains in crop yield or value of production, particularly in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_1, ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_mala24_5]; zai pits combined with stone lines in Burkina Faso are reported to raise sorghum yields by over 100% [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_3]; Ethiopian early adopters had a 15.2 percent higher value of production and invested plots 20.6 percent higher [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_4]; physical structures buffered crop growth against the 2015 severe drought in Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]; and dry spells can be bridged through water management [ev_crop_yield_rock10_1]. Programme reports add rainfed yield gains of 24% to 26% in Karnataka and 20.8% in Uttarakhand, yields rising from 0.5 to more than 1.2 t per hectare in wetter Mauritanian watersheds, and crop diversification from water harvesting with irrigation [ev_crop_yield_iegind11_1, ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_arega24_2]. Losses come from structures taking cropland and from excess water: in an Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, possibly through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. A meta-analysis of water-harvesting studies across semi-arid Africa and Asia finds crop yields 78% higher on average, with a large standard deviation and range; average maize gains were almost 3000 kg/ha in Asian studies against 400 kg/ha in African ones, and gains were significantly larger in study years with rainfall below 330 mm [ev_crop_yield_boum16_1, ev_crop_yield_boum16_6, ev_crop_yield_boum16_5, ev_crop_yield_boum16_4, ev_crop_yield_boum16_3]. In Burkina Faso stone rows or grass strips gave sorghum yield increases of 12–58%, particularly under poor rainfall (Zougmoré et al. 2004, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_23]; in Ethiopia's upper Agula watershed integrated catchment management combined with fertiliser and in-situ moisture conservation raised rainfed crop productivity by 50% (Alemayehu et al. 2009, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_10]; and a global hydrology–crop model suggested rainwater harvesting would raise overall crop production by 35% (Wisser et al. 2010) [ev_crop_yield_glen12_9].
conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The excess-water losses are held out of it as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Bunds should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. The evidence itself names what separates gains from losses. Rainfall: gains concentrate in low-rainfall or variable areas and in drier periods, while bunds lose yield in high-rainfall areas, and in Tigray bunds slightly raised productivity in drier periods but reduced it in moist seasons because cropped area was lost to the bunds [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_8, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]. Time and maintenance: value of production rose only after structures had been maintained for at least 7 years, later adopters saw no significant gain, and bunds cut yields in the first few years [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. Who decides: imposed structures often reduced cultivable area by 3 to 20% without improving productivity, and structures promoted mostly off-farm for community resource protection gave no gain [ev_crop_yield_roose94_5, ev_crop_yield_abate21_1]. Severity: dry spells can be bridged but yields cannot be sustained in a meteorological drought [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Practice: fanya juu and soil bunds account for the measured losses [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. The actionable distinctions are therefore siting by rainfall regime, farmer-owned rather than imposed structures, and a maintenance horizon of years. On quality, many of the largest gains are from bundled programmes or lender completion reports (Ethiopia public works, India watershed projects, Mauritania), with value of production and forage biomass used as proxies, while the losses come from an Ethiopian synthesis and a matched study; the drought finding is a secondary citation in a review [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_forage_productivity_mrt14_3, ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The nitrogen finding is a content on farm soils, not a yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The meta-analysis also holds losses: 21 of its observations show lower yields with water harvesting, most of them in-soil storage techniques [ev_crop_yield_boum16_2]. Without added nutrients, water-conservation measures in the Sahel had little influence on yields in years with well-distributed rainfall (Zougmoré et al. 2003b, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_17]. The Agula gain is bundled with fertiliser and measured before and after over decades, and the global figure is a model result that also projects reduced river flows [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_10, ev_crop_yield_glen12_9].

justification.pool_note: This row draws on 49 evidence unit(s) from 24 source(s); the weighting counts sources, not units, so several findings from one paper do not multiply its say.
justification.mechanism: Soil and water conservation and water harvesting have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains come from retaining moisture and soil: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 69% for soil and stone bunds and gains of 71.7% for maize and 68.2% for sorghum without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_7, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_8]; four studies in a systematic review find 20–24 per cent gains in crop yield or value of production, particularly in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_1, ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_mala24_5]; zai pits combined with stone lines in Burkina Faso are reported to raise sorghum yields by over 100% [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_3]; Ethiopian early adopters had a 15.2 percent higher value of production and invested plots 20.6 percent higher [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_4]; physical structures buffered crop growth against the 2015 severe drought in Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]; and dry spells can be bridged through water management [ev_crop_yield_rock10_1]. Programme reports add rainfed yield gains of 24% to 26% in Karnataka and 20.8% in Uttarakhand, yields rising from 0.5 to more than 1.2 t per hectare in wetter Mauritanian watersheds, and crop diversification from water harvesting with irrigation [ev_crop_yield_iegind11_1, ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_arega24_2]. Losses come from structures taking cropland and from excess water: in an Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, possibly through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. A meta-analysis of water-harvesting studies across semi-arid Africa and Asia finds crop yields 78% higher on average, with a large standard deviation and range; average maize gains were almost 3000 kg/ha in Asian studies against 400 kg/ha in African ones, and gains were significantly larger in study years with rainfall below 330 mm [ev_crop_yield_boum16_1, ev_crop_yield_boum16_6, ev_crop_yield_boum16_5, ev_crop_yield_boum16_4, ev_crop_yield_boum16_3]. In Burkina Faso stone rows or grass strips gave sorghum yield increases of 12–58%, particularly under poor rainfall (Zougmoré et al. 2004, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_23]; in Ethiopia's upper Agula watershed integrated catchment management combined with fertiliser and in-situ moisture conservation raised rainfed crop productivity by 50% (Alemayehu et al. 2009, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_10]; and a global hydrology–crop model suggested rainwater harvesting would raise overall crop production by 35% (Wisser et al. 2010) [ev_crop_yield_glen12_9].
justification.conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The excess-water losses are held out of it as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Bunds should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. The evidence itself names what separates gains from losses. Rainfall: gains concentrate in low-rainfall or variable areas and in drier periods, while bunds lose yield in high-rainfall areas, and in Tigray bunds slightly raised productivity in drier periods but reduced it in moist seasons because cropped area was lost to the bunds [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_8, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]. Time and maintenance: value of production rose only after structures had been maintained for at least 7 years, later adopters saw no significant gain, and bunds cut yields in the first few years [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. Who decides: imposed structures often reduced cultivable area by 3 to 20% without improving productivity, and structures promoted mostly off-farm for community resource protection gave no gain [ev_crop_yield_roose94_5, ev_crop_yield_abate21_1]. Severity: dry spells can be bridged but yields cannot be sustained in a meteorological drought [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Practice: fanya juu and soil bunds account for the measured losses [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. The actionable distinctions are therefore siting by rainfall regime, farmer-owned rather than imposed structures, and a maintenance horizon of years. On quality, many of the largest gains are from bundled programmes or lender completion reports (Ethiopia public works, India watershed projects, Mauritania), with value of production and forage biomass used as proxies, while the losses come from an Ethiopian synthesis and a matched study; the drought finding is a secondary citation in a review [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_forage_productivity_mrt14_3, ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The nitrogen finding is a content on farm soils, not a yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The meta-analysis also holds losses: 21 of its observations show lower yields with water harvesting, most of them in-soil storage techniques [ev_crop_yield_boum16_2]. Without added nutrients, water-conservation measures in the Sahel had little influence on yields in years with well-distributed rainfall (Zougmoré et al. 2003b, cited in a review) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_17]. The Agula gain is bundled with fertiliser and measured before and after over decades, and the global figure is a model result that also projects reduced river flows [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_10, ev_crop_yield_glen12_9].

effect_mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture outperforms conventional practice at median rainfall and clay even without fertiliser and gains more as seasons get drier [ev_crop_yield_stew18_4, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1] and a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. Primary trials acquired in the latest round add to this: in Nigeria, averaged over four years, sorghum grain yield rose by 16% under open ridging, 25% under tied ridging and 57% under tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch, and rainfall water use efficiency rose from 1.26 kg per hectare per mm on the flat bed to 1.97 under tied ridging with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_2, ev_crop_yield_chir06_1, ev_crop_yield_chir06_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]; Zambian basins averaged 4.4 t of maize per hectare against 1.7 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar12_1], and in Malawi conservation agriculture (planting in small holes under residue cover) gave 600 and 700 kg per hectare more grain than conventional ridge tillage, with lower yield variation [ev_crop_yield_seti18_2, ev_crop_yield_seti18_1, ev_yield_stability_seti18_3]. Nigerian sorghum under tied ridging with mulch fell below 1000 kg per hectare once in four years, against three times on the flat bed [ev_yield_stability_chir06_12]. Reviews add second-hand gains: tied ridges doubling maize yield on sandy soils in Zimbabwe (Motsi et al., 2004), tied ridging with mineral fertiliser raising maize grain yield from 1 to 6 Mg per hectare in semi-arid Tanzania (Jensen et al., 2003), tied ridges improving barley grain yield by at least 44% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), basin tillage with mulching raising maize yields by 30–50% on a South African clay (Hensley et al., 2000; Walker et al., 2005), soil bunds giving at least 30% more lowland rice in Tanzania in normal years (Raes et al., 2007), zaï giving 0.3–0.4 Mg per hectare in a year of low rainfall where land without pits gave 0 (Kaboré and Reij, 2004), and in situ water harvesting raising yields on reclaimed degraded farmland in Burkina Faso by at least 400 kg/ha (Reij et al., 2009) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_10, ev_crop_yield_dile13_5, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14, ev_crop_yield_dile13_7, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_9, ev_crop_yield_dile13_3, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_12, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_16, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_3, ev_crop_yield_dile13_8]. On grazing land, contour bunds in Ugandan pastures increased fodder availability (Ngigi, 2003), and saltbush planted in furrows upslope of ridges in Jordan was reported to considerably improve forage quantity and quality (Akroush et al., 2011; Al-Shamiri and Ziadat, 2012) [ev_forage_productivity_biaz12_25, ev_forage_productivity_stav20_5].
conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect in a Kenyan season with a failed start, tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; and the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The newer primaries also show where the gain fails: Nigerian open and tied ridging without mulch yielded 9 and 3% less than the flat bed in 2000, when rain failed at flowering and grain filling, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency without a residue mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]; in Ghana tied ridges made no significant difference to maize yield [ev_crop_yield_dalt14_1]; and in Mozambique basin and direct-seeded maize yields did not differ [ev_crop_yield_kida19_1]. Much of the size rides on mulch or fertiliser: in Nigeria mulch on a flat bed alone raised yield by 77%, more than any ridging arm [ev_crop_yield_chir06_4], and the Tanzanian tied-ridge figure compares ridges with fertiliser against flat planting without it [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14]. The review figures are cited second-hand and several multipliers come without a baseline yield.

justification.mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture outperforms conventional practice at median rainfall and clay even without fertiliser and gains more as seasons get drier [ev_crop_yield_stew18_4, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1] and a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. Primary trials acquired in the latest round add to this: in Nigeria, averaged over four years, sorghum grain yield rose by 16% under open ridging, 25% under tied ridging and 57% under tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch, and rainfall water use efficiency rose from 1.26 kg per hectare per mm on the flat bed to 1.97 under tied ridging with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_2, ev_crop_yield_chir06_1, ev_crop_yield_chir06_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]; Zambian basins averaged 4.4 t of maize per hectare against 1.7 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar12_1], and in Malawi conservation agriculture (planting in small holes under residue cover) gave 600 and 700 kg per hectare more grain than conventional ridge tillage, with lower yield variation [ev_crop_yield_seti18_2, ev_crop_yield_seti18_1, ev_yield_stability_seti18_3]. Nigerian sorghum under tied ridging with mulch fell below 1000 kg per hectare once in four years, against three times on the flat bed [ev_yield_stability_chir06_12]. Reviews add second-hand gains: tied ridges doubling maize yield on sandy soils in Zimbabwe (Motsi et al., 2004), tied ridging with mineral fertiliser raising maize grain yield from 1 to 6 Mg per hectare in semi-arid Tanzania (Jensen et al., 2003), tied ridges improving barley grain yield by at least 44% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), basin tillage with mulching raising maize yields by 30–50% on a South African clay (Hensley et al., 2000; Walker et al., 2005), soil bunds giving at least 30% more lowland rice in Tanzania in normal years (Raes et al., 2007), zaï giving 0.3–0.4 Mg per hectare in a year of low rainfall where land without pits gave 0 (Kaboré and Reij, 2004), and in situ water harvesting raising yields on reclaimed degraded farmland in Burkina Faso by at least 400 kg/ha (Reij et al., 2009) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_10, ev_crop_yield_dile13_5, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14, ev_crop_yield_dile13_7, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_9, ev_crop_yield_dile13_3, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_12, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_16, ev_crop_yield_biaz12_3, ev_crop_yield_dile13_8]. On grazing land, contour bunds in Ugandan pastures increased fodder availability (Ngigi, 2003), and saltbush planted in furrows upslope of ridges in Jordan was reported to considerably improve forage quantity and quality (Akroush et al., 2011; Al-Shamiri and Ziadat, 2012) [ev_forage_productivity_biaz12_25, ev_forage_productivity_stav20_5].
justification.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect in a Kenyan season with a failed start, tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; and the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The newer primaries also show where the gain fails: Nigerian open and tied ridging without mulch yielded 9 and 3% less than the flat bed in 2000, when rain failed at flowering and grain filling, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency without a residue mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]; in Ghana tied ridges made no significant difference to maize yield [ev_crop_yield_dalt14_1]; and in Mozambique basin and direct-seeded maize yields did not differ [ev_crop_yield_kida19_1]. Much of the size rides on mulch or fertiliser: in Nigeria mulch on a flat bed alone raised yield by 77%, more than any ridging arm [ev_crop_yield_chir06_4], and the Tanzanian tied-ridge figure compares ridges with fertiliser against flat planting without it [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_14]. The review figures are cited second-hand and several multipliers come without a baseline yield.

effect_mechanism: Semi-circular bunds, Vallerani micro-catchments and half-moons harvest runoff for crops and grasses. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost gave 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. A review tabulates crop yield increases of 50–200% from half-moons in Burkina Faso and Niger, and cites micro-basin water harvesting in Zambia doubling maize yields to 3 t per hectare [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. Negarim micro-catchments with supplementary irrigation supported fruit production at Embrapa Semi-Arid in Brazil, and semi-circular bunds raised millet grain production under African conditions [ev_crop_yield_fao13c_2, ev_crop_yield_fao13c_1]. For the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso the WOCAT compiler reports more fodder in quantity and quality, a surplus of 22–106 grazing days per tropical cattle unit per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1528_2012_animal_production].
conditionality: Animal production was rated lower on the Niger sheets because treated rangeland must be protected from grazing for the first years while vegetation establishes [ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1613_2014_animal_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1614_2014_animal_production]. The Burkina Faso half-moon contrast is against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so it measures bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. The FAO manual cites earlier work, the review figures are ranges and single citations rather than pooled estimates, and the WOCAT units are practitioner judgements [ev_crop_yield_fao13c_1, ev_crop_yield_fao13c_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5].
