effect_mechanism: Sand dams, small reservoirs, subsurface dams, farm ponds, check dams and haffirs store runoff that farmers use to irrigate more land and take a second or dry-season crop, while sediment trapped behind check dams can be planted with fodder; in Kenya sand-dam water lets farmers irrigate more crops and raise production, and in Brazil soil management in subsurface dams raised crop productivity [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_crop_yield_brito07_5, ev_crop_yield_wocat_2844_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6716_2023_fodder_production]. WOCAT compilers in Somalia describe reliable irrigation from a haffir improving tomato and watermelon, grasses regenerating around the dam, and better water and fodder raising animal production, while a second Somali sheet credits stone lines, rock check dams and gabions with better moisture retention on farmland and more grazing [ev_crop_yield_wocat_7777_2026_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_animal_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_7778_2026_crop_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7778_2026_animal_production]. Sand dams in Kenya cut crop failure against a control catchment, and in Zimbabwe improved water availability improved livestock health where cattle had been driven up to 20 km to water [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Stored water also stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, reviews report rainwater harvesting systems stabilising production under intra-seasonal rainfall variability and supplemental irrigation of 50–200 mm bridging critical dry spells, wheat output in Pakistan rose from 450 to 815 kg over seven years after small reservoirs were built, a bundle of moisture conservation, rainwater harvesting and micro-irrigation in India raised system productivity by 25%, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_yield_stability_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_rock10_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. In Rwanda, runoff from the terrace waterways collected in a dug, lined pond and applied to maize by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation gave 11982 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. Trials of supplemental irrigation from stored runoff now measure the gain directly. In Burkina Faso, sorghum under the farmer's normal practice averaged 455 kg per hectare over 3 years, against 712 with supplemental irrigation alone and 1403 with irrigation plus fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_1, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_2]; a model of the same kind of system puts the long-term average gain from supplemental irrigation at 150%, or 450 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. In Kenya, maize with supplemental irrigation from a runoff dam plus fertiliser averaged 1796 kg per hectare against 1375 without irrigation, with the steadiest yields (a coefficient of variation of 5% against 11% for the farmers' control) and more grain per mm of rain and irrigation (4.1 against 2.1 kg per mm per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_barr05_1, ev_yield_stability_barr05_8, ev_rain_water_productivity_barr05_9]. In Pakistan, supplemental irrigation from harvested rainwater raised yields over adjacent rainfed fields by 146% for wheat, 101% for mustard, 118% for maize and 101% for pearl millet [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_2, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_3, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_4]. On China's Loess Plateau, cropland formed behind silted check dams is reported to produce 2 to 3 times more food than terraced cropland and 6 to 10 times more than sloping cropland (Jin et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2011) [ev_crop_yield_shi19_5], and in semi-arid Zimbabwe supplementary irrigation from ex-situ water harvesting raised water productivity from 1.75 to 2.3 kg per cubic metre (Kahinda et al. 2007) [ev_rain_water_productivity_dile13_6, ev_rain_water_productivity_biaz12_5]. In a Burkina Faso farm-pond trial, sorghum given supplemental irrigation from the harvested runoff yielded 680 against 443 kg per hectare in 1999 and 1138 against 634 kg per hectare in 2000, both seasons with serious dry spells [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_4, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_5]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial (Barron and Okwach), supplemental irrigation from a runoff-fed earth dam plus fertiliser raised maize yields over fertilised plots without irrigation in low-rainfall seasons (<300 mm) but not in seasons above 300 mm, and in a dry long-rains season only the irrigated plots produced any grain at all [ev_crop_yield_barr05_3, ev_crop_yield_barr05_4].
conditionality: The WOCAT units are practitioner ratings from technology sheets, and the literature units are largely reviews citing earlier studies, an expert's personal communication on livestock, and Brazilian case accounts from an upper-middle-income setting [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_livestock_productivity_veno12_1, ev_crop_yield_cirilo03_4]. A Brazilian subsurface dam produced no harvest in a year of adverse weather [ev_crop_yield_brito07_6]; fodder and livestock outcomes enter only as components of the production gap. The Kenyan and Zimbabwean sand-dam findings come from interviews and respondent statements [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Soil salinisation may appear on check-dam farmland, the Pakistani wheat figure has no area denominator, the Indian productivity gain bundles micro-irrigation, and the pond figures come from a farmer survey reported in a preprint [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The irrigation gain depends on inputs and the season. Supplemental irrigation without fertiliser did not raise Kenyan maize yields, and in the first Burkina Faso season, with good rainfall distribution, irrigated and non-irrigated plots did not differ significantly, fertiliser being the main reason for higher yields that year [ev_crop_yield_barr05_2, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_3]. In good-rainfall Kenyan seasons (>350 mm) irrigation had no or slightly adverse effects on final yields [ev_crop_yield_barr05_7], and overall water-use efficiency of rain plus irrigation did not rise with irrigation in Burkina Faso [ev_rain_water_productivity_foxr03_6]. In Tigray, irrigation chiefly from water-harvesting schemes raised output risk when used alone and lowered it only in combination with improved seed and fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_kato11_8]. The Burkina Faso model adds that the yield gain from supplemental irrigation alone does not pay back the labour and capital invested [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. The Pakistani gains compare irrigated with adjacent rainfed fields rather than a randomised control, and the Loess Plateau multipliers are second-hand, with no baseline yield [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_shi19_5]. In the Kenyan dam trial's drought season the catchment yielded no runoff to irrigate with, both biomass and grain were strongly hit by the lack of water, and no treatment differed from another [ev_crop_yield_barr05_5].

justification.mechanism: Sand dams, small reservoirs, subsurface dams, farm ponds, check dams and haffirs store runoff that farmers use to irrigate more land and take a second or dry-season crop, while sediment trapped behind check dams can be planted with fodder; in Kenya sand-dam water lets farmers irrigate more crops and raise production, and in Brazil soil management in subsurface dams raised crop productivity [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_crop_yield_brito07_5, ev_crop_yield_wocat_2844_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6716_2023_fodder_production]. WOCAT compilers in Somalia describe reliable irrigation from a haffir improving tomato and watermelon, grasses regenerating around the dam, and better water and fodder raising animal production, while a second Somali sheet credits stone lines, rock check dams and gabions with better moisture retention on farmland and more grazing [ev_crop_yield_wocat_7777_2026_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_animal_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_7778_2026_crop_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7778_2026_animal_production]. Sand dams in Kenya cut crop failure against a control catchment, and in Zimbabwe improved water availability improved livestock health where cattle had been driven up to 20 km to water [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Stored water also stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, reviews report rainwater harvesting systems stabilising production under intra-seasonal rainfall variability and supplemental irrigation of 50–200 mm bridging critical dry spells, wheat output in Pakistan rose from 450 to 815 kg over seven years after small reservoirs were built, a bundle of moisture conservation, rainwater harvesting and micro-irrigation in India raised system productivity by 25%, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_yield_stability_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_rock10_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. In Rwanda, runoff from the terrace waterways collected in a dug, lined pond and applied to maize by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation gave 11982 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. Trials of supplemental irrigation from stored runoff now measure the gain directly. In Burkina Faso, sorghum under the farmer's normal practice averaged 455 kg per hectare over 3 years, against 712 with supplemental irrigation alone and 1403 with irrigation plus fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_1, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_2]; a model of the same kind of system puts the long-term average gain from supplemental irrigation at 150%, or 450 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. In Kenya, maize with supplemental irrigation from a runoff dam plus fertiliser averaged 1796 kg per hectare against 1375 without irrigation, with the steadiest yields (a coefficient of variation of 5% against 11% for the farmers' control) and more grain per mm of rain and irrigation (4.1 against 2.1 kg per mm per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_barr05_1, ev_yield_stability_barr05_8, ev_rain_water_productivity_barr05_9]. In Pakistan, supplemental irrigation from harvested rainwater raised yields over adjacent rainfed fields by 146% for wheat, 101% for mustard, 118% for maize and 101% for pearl millet [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_2, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_3, ev_crop_yield_waqa25_4]. On China's Loess Plateau, cropland formed behind silted check dams is reported to produce 2 to 3 times more food than terraced cropland and 6 to 10 times more than sloping cropland (Jin et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2011) [ev_crop_yield_shi19_5], and in semi-arid Zimbabwe supplementary irrigation from ex-situ water harvesting raised water productivity from 1.75 to 2.3 kg per cubic metre (Kahinda et al. 2007) [ev_rain_water_productivity_dile13_6, ev_rain_water_productivity_biaz12_5]. In a Burkina Faso farm-pond trial, sorghum given supplemental irrigation from the harvested runoff yielded 680 against 443 kg per hectare in 1999 and 1138 against 634 kg per hectare in 2000, both seasons with serious dry spells [ev_crop_yield_foxr03_4, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_5]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial (Barron and Okwach), supplemental irrigation from a runoff-fed earth dam plus fertiliser raised maize yields over fertilised plots without irrigation in low-rainfall seasons (<300 mm) but not in seasons above 300 mm, and in a dry long-rains season only the irrigated plots produced any grain at all [ev_crop_yield_barr05_3, ev_crop_yield_barr05_4].
justification.conditionality: The WOCAT units are practitioner ratings from technology sheets, and the literature units are largely reviews citing earlier studies, an expert's personal communication on livestock, and Brazilian case accounts from an upper-middle-income setting [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_livestock_productivity_veno12_1, ev_crop_yield_cirilo03_4]. A Brazilian subsurface dam produced no harvest in a year of adverse weather [ev_crop_yield_brito07_6]; fodder and livestock outcomes enter only as components of the production gap. The Kenyan and Zimbabwean sand-dam findings come from interviews and respondent statements [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Soil salinisation may appear on check-dam farmland, the Pakistani wheat figure has no area denominator, the Indian productivity gain bundles micro-irrigation, and the pond figures come from a farmer survey reported in a preprint [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The irrigation gain depends on inputs and the season. Supplemental irrigation without fertiliser did not raise Kenyan maize yields, and in the first Burkina Faso season, with good rainfall distribution, irrigated and non-irrigated plots did not differ significantly, fertiliser being the main reason for higher yields that year [ev_crop_yield_barr05_2, ev_crop_yield_foxr03_3]. In good-rainfall Kenyan seasons (>350 mm) irrigation had no or slightly adverse effects on final yields [ev_crop_yield_barr05_7], and overall water-use efficiency of rain plus irrigation did not rise with irrigation in Burkina Faso [ev_rain_water_productivity_foxr03_6]. In Tigray, irrigation chiefly from water-harvesting schemes raised output risk when used alone and lowered it only in combination with improved seed and fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_kato11_8]. The Burkina Faso model adds that the yield gain from supplemental irrigation alone does not pay back the labour and capital invested [ev_crop_yield_fox05_1]. The Pakistani gains compare irrigated with adjacent rainfed fields rather than a randomised control, and the Loess Plateau multipliers are second-hand, with no baseline yield [ev_crop_yield_waqa25_1, ev_crop_yield_shi19_5]. In the Kenyan dam trial's drought season the catchment yielded no runoff to irrigate with, both biomass and grain were strongly hit by the lack of water, and no treatment differed from another [ev_crop_yield_barr05_5].

effect_mechanism: Water-spreading weirs in Ethiopia, spate irrigation in Eritrea and marab floodplain farming in Jordan divert and spread floodwater over fields: the Ethiopian compiler states it is the expert's conviction that crop production increased with water harvested and spread over the farm as spate or supplementary irrigation to the seasonal rainfall [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6715_2023_crop_production]. Much of the gain goes to livestock: in Jordan the barley is mostly used to feed animals and the stubble is grazed, in Eritrea residues are fed to livestock, and in Ethiopia fodder rises with the soil and moisture conserved behind the structure, with animal production increasing as feed becomes more available [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_5770_2020_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1333_2010_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6715_2023_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_6715_2023_animal_production].
conditionality: Every unit is a practitioner rating from a WOCAT technology sheet; there is no literature measurement in this cell, and the Ethiopian crop rating is stated as the expert's conviction rather than a yield comparison [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6715_2023_crop_production]. Most of the remaining support is for fodder and animal production rather than food crops, which is why the class is only slight [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_5770_2020_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1333_2010_fodder_production].

effect_mechanism: Terraces, fanya juu and contour stone bunds or lines level slopes and slow runoff so more water and soil stay on the field; yields of maize, barley, millet and sorghum rose on terraced or bunded land, especially in dry years. Stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% in Burkina Faso and by about 142% with compost, and millet yields in Niger rose by more than 40% up to 15 years after the bunds were built [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_1_s]. WOCAT compilers add that stone lines in Tunisia protect farmland from degradation and contour stone bunds in Bhutan enlarge the cultivable area as stones are removed [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6610_2022_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_6891_2023_crop_production]. Meta-analyses support the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a 48% yield increase for terraces, an Ethiopian synthesis a mean gain of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds with soil total nitrogen up from 0.16 to 0.20%, and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1], and 2 to 4-year old bench terraces in Peru gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]; reviewed studies also report maize yields up nearly 50% on fanya juu terraces in semi-arid Kenya, wheat yields 6–7 times higher on stone-wall terraces than on slopes under the same input costs, and land productivity over 19% higher on bench terraces [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_4, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3, ev_agricultural_production_value_wei16_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. New primaries from Ethiopia add measured contrasts: terraced fields in the Anjene catchment gave 0.95, 1.86 and 1.73 t of teff, barley and maize per hectare against 0.49, 0.61 and 0.77 t on un-terraced farms, and improved water productivity by at least 100% [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]; plot-level econometrics found a yield premium for conserved plots in low-rainfall Tigray of ETB 412 or 299 per hectare depending on the estimator, and robust impacts of all the soil and water conservation technologies studied on crop output in low-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_1]. Bunds also steady output: soil bunds reduced production risk in low-rainfall areas, stone bunds did so when combined with inorganic fertilizer, and all the technologies studied reduced risk in high-rainfall areas [ev_yield_stability_kato11_3, ev_yield_stability_kato11_7, ev_yield_stability_kato11_5]. Reviews cite sorghum straw and grain yields doubled on plots with stone lines in Burkina Faso (Zougmore et al., 2000; Zougmoré et al., 2003) and stone bunds and terraces raising crop yield in Ethiopia by up to 53% (Nyssen et al., 2007; Gebremichael et al., 2005), with a survey in Dogu'a Tembien giving 0.65 t per hectare after physical conservation against 0.58 before (Nyssen et al., 2007) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_13, ev_crop_yield_dile13_4, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_2, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_12].
conditionality: Some literature figures are lender self-reports (Rwanda before/after yields, Indian with/without models bundled with crop packages); the Rwanda value-of-harvest gain is from an independent DIME evaluation, and the Burkina Faso and Niger gains are cited from earlier studies, the largest bundled with compost [ev_crop_yield_rwa18_7, ev_crop_yield_utk22_8, ev_agricultural_production_value_rwa18_3, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4]. Diversion banquettes in Niger reduced yields, progressive terraces on poor soils in Rwanda gave no yield increase, bench terraces need heavy fertility restoration before yields rise, and a Haitian compiler notes that on very degraded land farmers must wait for the soil to recover [ev_crop_yield_heusch95_1, ev_crop_yield_roose06_3, ev_crop_yield_roose94_4, ev_crop_yield_wocat_3223_2017_crop_production]. The Tunisian, Bhutanese and Haitian units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT sheets rather than measurements. Stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_9], and in Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. The terracing meta-analysis pools unweighted ratios and some of the largest multiples are single studies cited in reviews [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3]. The Burkina Faso rock-bund gain is for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. That is a compiler judgement for a group spanning earth bunds, stone lines, vegetative strips and fanya juu terraces, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. The same Ethiopian studies show the limit in wetter highlands: in high-rainfall Amhara conserved plots showed no significant yield difference, the point estimate lying ETB 179 or 145 per hectare below non-conserved plots, and only waterways and trees had robust impacts on output in high-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_2]. Earlier studies found fanya juu, soil and stone bunds and grass strips did not increase crop yield and biomass in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea (Herweg and Ludi, 1999; Kassie et al., 2008) [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_12]. Stone bunds alone had no independent risk-reducing effect in low-rainfall areas, and soil bunds raised production risk in Tigray, the driest region studied [ev_yield_stability_kato11_4, ev_yield_stability_kato11_6]. Rodents sheltering in narrowly spaced stone bunds can damage up to 225 kg of crop per hectare (Meheretu et al., 2014) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_4]. The Anjene terraces have been maintained for decades and farmers there also apply fertiliser on cereals, so the gap is not the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1].

justification.pool_note: This row draws on 53 evidence unit(s) from 25 source(s); the weighting counts sources, not units, so several findings from one paper do not multiply its say.
justification.mechanism: Terraces, fanya juu and contour stone bunds or lines level slopes and slow runoff so more water and soil stay on the field; yields of maize, barley, millet and sorghum rose on terraced or bunded land, especially in dry years. Stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% in Burkina Faso and by about 142% with compost, and millet yields in Niger rose by more than 40% up to 15 years after the bunds were built [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_1_s]. WOCAT compilers add that stone lines in Tunisia protect farmland from degradation and contour stone bunds in Bhutan enlarge the cultivable area as stones are removed [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6610_2022_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_6891_2023_crop_production]. Meta-analyses support the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a 48% yield increase for terraces, an Ethiopian synthesis a mean gain of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds with soil total nitrogen up from 0.16 to 0.20%, and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1], and 2 to 4-year old bench terraces in Peru gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]; reviewed studies also report maize yields up nearly 50% on fanya juu terraces in semi-arid Kenya, wheat yields 6–7 times higher on stone-wall terraces than on slopes under the same input costs, and land productivity over 19% higher on bench terraces [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_4, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3, ev_agricultural_production_value_wei16_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. New primaries from Ethiopia add measured contrasts: terraced fields in the Anjene catchment gave 0.95, 1.86 and 1.73 t of teff, barley and maize per hectare against 0.49, 0.61 and 0.77 t on un-terraced farms, and improved water productivity by at least 100% [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_2, ev_crop_yield_adgo13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_adgo13_7]; plot-level econometrics found a yield premium for conserved plots in low-rainfall Tigray of ETB 412 or 299 per hectare depending on the estimator, and robust impacts of all the soil and water conservation technologies studied on crop output in low-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_1]. Bunds also steady output: soil bunds reduced production risk in low-rainfall areas, stone bunds did so when combined with inorganic fertilizer, and all the technologies studied reduced risk in high-rainfall areas [ev_yield_stability_kato11_3, ev_yield_stability_kato11_7, ev_yield_stability_kato11_5]. Reviews cite sorghum straw and grain yields doubled on plots with stone lines in Burkina Faso (Zougmore et al., 2000; Zougmoré et al., 2003) and stone bunds and terraces raising crop yield in Ethiopia by up to 53% (Nyssen et al., 2007; Gebremichael et al., 2005), with a survey in Dogu'a Tembien giving 0.65 t per hectare after physical conservation against 0.58 before (Nyssen et al., 2007) [ev_crop_yield_biaz12_13, ev_crop_yield_dile13_4, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_2, ev_crop_yield_gebr18_12].
justification.conditionality: Some literature figures are lender self-reports (Rwanda before/after yields, Indian with/without models bundled with crop packages); the Rwanda value-of-harvest gain is from an independent DIME evaluation, and the Burkina Faso and Niger gains are cited from earlier studies, the largest bundled with compost [ev_crop_yield_rwa18_7, ev_crop_yield_utk22_8, ev_agricultural_production_value_rwa18_3, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4]. Diversion banquettes in Niger reduced yields, progressive terraces on poor soils in Rwanda gave no yield increase, bench terraces need heavy fertility restoration before yields rise, and a Haitian compiler notes that on very degraded land farmers must wait for the soil to recover [ev_crop_yield_heusch95_1, ev_crop_yield_roose06_3, ev_crop_yield_roose94_4, ev_crop_yield_wocat_3223_2017_crop_production]. The Tunisian, Bhutanese and Haitian units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT sheets rather than measurements. Stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_9], and in Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. The terracing meta-analysis pools unweighted ratios and some of the largest multiples are single studies cited in reviews [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3]. The Burkina Faso rock-bund gain is for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. That is a compiler judgement for a group spanning earth bunds, stone lines, vegetative strips and fanya juu terraces, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. The same Ethiopian studies show the limit in wetter highlands: in high-rainfall Amhara conserved plots showed no significant yield difference, the point estimate lying ETB 179 or 145 per hectare below non-conserved plots, and only waterways and trees had robust impacts on output in high-rainfall areas [ev_agricultural_production_value_kass08_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_kato11_2]. Earlier studies found fanya juu, soil and stone bunds and grass strips did not increase crop yield and biomass in the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea (Herweg and Ludi, 1999; Kassie et al., 2008) [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_12]. Stone bunds alone had no independent risk-reducing effect in low-rainfall areas, and soil bunds raised production risk in Tigray, the driest region studied [ev_yield_stability_kato11_4, ev_yield_stability_kato11_6]. Rodents sheltering in narrowly spaced stone bunds can damage up to 225 kg of crop per hectare (Meheretu et al., 2014) [ev_crop_yield_gebr18_4]. The Anjene terraces have been maintained for decades and farmers there also apply fertiliser on cereals, so the gap is not the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_adgo13_1].

effect_mechanism: Water harvesting and soil and water conservation raise household income and returns through higher and steadier yields, dry-season irrigation of higher-value crops and better fodder and livestock, but the evidence also shows them failing to pay. On the gain side, a quasi-experimental study cited in a review found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]; in Kenya, farmers living near sand dams saw average income rise by 60% [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports net present values of 3486.2 Birr per hectare for stone bunds, 2794.0 for bench terraces and 5283.4 for level fanya juu [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_economic_return_adim16_3]; Zambian crop budgets give hand-hoe conservation-farming basins returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation for cotton [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6]; first-year Zimbabwean planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; and Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In the Ethiopian highlands, teff, barley and maize on long-established terraces earned incremental income of US$ 159, 275 and 141 per hectare per year over un-terraced farms, and terrace investment for barley had an average net present value of US$ 1542 over 50 years at a 10% discount rate [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4, ev_economic_return_adgo13_5, ev_economic_return_adgo13_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_10]. A risk and cost-benefit analysis of farm ponds for supplemental irrigation, combined with fertiliser and an off-season tomato crop, gives net profits of 151–626 USD per hectare per year in Burkina Faso and 109–477 in Kenya, depending on labour opportunity cost [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_fox05_4]. In a Kenyan trial, unmulched and straw-mulched ridge-furrow rain harvesting raised wheat net income by 82% and 117% over flat planting [ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. Switching to conservation-agriculture basins in Zambia gave a marginal rate of return of 860% over hand hoeing and 360% over ploughing, and in Mozambique basin net returns were $148 against $104 per hectare under conventional tillage [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3, ev_economic_return_kida19_2, ev_economic_return_kida19_4]. Reviews cite more: Hatibu et al. (2006) found road-catchment rainwater harvesting for paddy in Tanzania returning more than US$ 12 per person-day against US$ 3.7 for rainfed sorghum, Ngigi et al. (2005) farm ponds in Kenya raising annual maize returns by 150%, Senkondo et al. (2004) rainwater harvesting in Tanzania profitable in the long term, Awulachew et al. (2008) users of water-management techniques earning significantly more agricultural income than non-users, and Gebremedhin et al. (1999) stone bunds returning 50% [ev_economic_return_biaz12_21, ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_biaz12_19, ev_household_income_biaz12_18, ev_economic_return_gebr18_3]. In Apurímac, Peru, Cárdenas et al. cite a study by Tafur for a benefit of 1.96 soles per sol invested in building cochas [ev_economic_return_card22_1]; in Pakistan, farmers earned a net income of US$ 1799 from fish farming in a rainwater-harvesting farm pond, and maize irrigated from harvested rainwater had a cumulative benefit-cost ratio of 2.02 by the second year [ev_household_income_waqa25_7, ev_economic_return_waqa25_5]. A meta-analysis puts the payback of water-harvesting investment at 4–5 years at the pooled-average maize yield gain [ev_economic_return_boum16_8]. WOCAT compilers mostly rate farm income as increased [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income, ev_household_income_wocat_2844_2017_farm_income]. On the loss side, Ethiopian graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds had net present values below zero of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], single soil and water conservation measures in Burkina Faso did not cover their annual costs [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3], Brazil's production-cistern programme returned a benefit-cost ratio of 0.0858 over its evaluation window [ev_economic_return_casag22_9], and in a Nigerian trial tied and open ridging, with or without mulch, made net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12% because of high production costs [ev_economic_return_chir06_10]. Zougmoré et al. (2004), cited by Biazin et al., found stone rows and grass strips in Burkina Faso not cost-effective without added nutrients despite sorghum yield gains of 12–58% [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24], and in Pakistan pearl millet irrigated from harvested rainwater had a benefit-cost ratio of −0.49 in its first year, still 0.53 by the third [ev_economic_return_waqa25_6].
conditionality: The roll-up states conflicting evidence because the sub-practice rows disagree: the runoff-catchment, micro-catchment and terracing rows lean towards gains, while the in-field and cross-family rows are each split. What separates the sides is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1], but a Zimbabwe household panel that holds inputs constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]; in a Kenyan drought season net benefits were higher without tied ridging [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]. Complementary inputs and crop value separate them too: in Burkina Faso, supplemental irrigation from a farm pond alone did not repay the heavy labour and capital invested, and paid only with fertiliser and a high-value tomato crop [ev_economic_return_fox05_2, ev_economic_return_fox05_3]; stone rows and grass strips paid only with nutrients added [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24]; in Pakistan stored water paid on maize but not on pearl millet [ev_economic_return_waqa25_5, ev_economic_return_waqa25_6]; and the Tanzanian paddy return is high because paddy cannot be grown there without rainwater harvesting at all [ev_economic_return_biaz12_21]. Region matters: the meta-analysis puts payback at 2 years for the average Asian farmer but more than 15 years for the average African farmer, at world maize prices [ev_economic_return_boum16_7]. In Mozambique basins did not differ significantly in net return from conventional tillage at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3], while in Ghana tied ridges with grass strips returned more than flat land in 2010 but not in 2011 [ev_economic_return_dalt14_3]. Farm size also matters: the Brazilian cistern income effect was confined to small farms and reversed on farms larger than 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5, ev_household_income_casag22_6]. Much of the literature comes from bundled programmes, lender reports and secondary citations, the Fox and meta-analysis returns are modelled, the Kenyan ridge-furrow net-income gains are from a single field trial, and the Tanzanian, Kenyan pond and stone-bund figures are cited in reviews [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_boum16_8, ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_biaz12_20]; the Indian pond returns are cross-sectional and confounded by farm size, and sand dams are judged likely not cost-efficient [ev_economic_return_pals23_1, ev_economic_return_ritc21_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty, and few studies follow households over time.

justification.mechanism: Water harvesting and soil and water conservation raise household income and returns through higher and steadier yields, dry-season irrigation of higher-value crops and better fodder and livestock, but the evidence also shows them failing to pay. On the gain side, a quasi-experimental study cited in a review found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]; in Kenya, farmers living near sand dams saw average income rise by 60% [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports net present values of 3486.2 Birr per hectare for stone bunds, 2794.0 for bench terraces and 5283.4 for level fanya juu [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_economic_return_adim16_3]; Zambian crop budgets give hand-hoe conservation-farming basins returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation for cotton [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6]; first-year Zimbabwean planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; and Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In the Ethiopian highlands, teff, barley and maize on long-established terraces earned incremental income of US$ 159, 275 and 141 per hectare per year over un-terraced farms, and terrace investment for barley had an average net present value of US$ 1542 over 50 years at a 10% discount rate [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4, ev_economic_return_adgo13_5, ev_economic_return_adgo13_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_10]. A risk and cost-benefit analysis of farm ponds for supplemental irrigation, combined with fertiliser and an off-season tomato crop, gives net profits of 151–626 USD per hectare per year in Burkina Faso and 109–477 in Kenya, depending on labour opportunity cost [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_fox05_4]. In a Kenyan trial, unmulched and straw-mulched ridge-furrow rain harvesting raised wheat net income by 82% and 117% over flat planting [ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. Switching to conservation-agriculture basins in Zambia gave a marginal rate of return of 860% over hand hoeing and 360% over ploughing, and in Mozambique basin net returns were $148 against $104 per hectare under conventional tillage [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3, ev_economic_return_kida19_2, ev_economic_return_kida19_4]. Reviews cite more: Hatibu et al. (2006) found road-catchment rainwater harvesting for paddy in Tanzania returning more than US$ 12 per person-day against US$ 3.7 for rainfed sorghum, Ngigi et al. (2005) farm ponds in Kenya raising annual maize returns by 150%, Senkondo et al. (2004) rainwater harvesting in Tanzania profitable in the long term, Awulachew et al. (2008) users of water-management techniques earning significantly more agricultural income than non-users, and Gebremedhin et al. (1999) stone bunds returning 50% [ev_economic_return_biaz12_21, ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_biaz12_19, ev_household_income_biaz12_18, ev_economic_return_gebr18_3]. In Apurímac, Peru, Cárdenas et al. cite a study by Tafur for a benefit of 1.96 soles per sol invested in building cochas [ev_economic_return_card22_1]; in Pakistan, farmers earned a net income of US$ 1799 from fish farming in a rainwater-harvesting farm pond, and maize irrigated from harvested rainwater had a cumulative benefit-cost ratio of 2.02 by the second year [ev_household_income_waqa25_7, ev_economic_return_waqa25_5]. A meta-analysis puts the payback of water-harvesting investment at 4–5 years at the pooled-average maize yield gain [ev_economic_return_boum16_8]. WOCAT compilers mostly rate farm income as increased [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income, ev_household_income_wocat_2844_2017_farm_income]. On the loss side, Ethiopian graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds had net present values below zero of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], single soil and water conservation measures in Burkina Faso did not cover their annual costs [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3], Brazil's production-cistern programme returned a benefit-cost ratio of 0.0858 over its evaluation window [ev_economic_return_casag22_9], and in a Nigerian trial tied and open ridging, with or without mulch, made net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12% because of high production costs [ev_economic_return_chir06_10]. Zougmoré et al. (2004), cited by Biazin et al., found stone rows and grass strips in Burkina Faso not cost-effective without added nutrients despite sorghum yield gains of 12–58% [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24], and in Pakistan pearl millet irrigated from harvested rainwater had a benefit-cost ratio of −0.49 in its first year, still 0.53 by the third [ev_economic_return_waqa25_6].
justification.conditionality: The roll-up states conflicting evidence because the sub-practice rows disagree: the runoff-catchment, micro-catchment and terracing rows lean towards gains, while the in-field and cross-family rows are each split. What separates the sides is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1], but a Zimbabwe household panel that holds inputs constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]; in a Kenyan drought season net benefits were higher without tied ridging [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]. Complementary inputs and crop value separate them too: in Burkina Faso, supplemental irrigation from a farm pond alone did not repay the heavy labour and capital invested, and paid only with fertiliser and a high-value tomato crop [ev_economic_return_fox05_2, ev_economic_return_fox05_3]; stone rows and grass strips paid only with nutrients added [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24]; in Pakistan stored water paid on maize but not on pearl millet [ev_economic_return_waqa25_5, ev_economic_return_waqa25_6]; and the Tanzanian paddy return is high because paddy cannot be grown there without rainwater harvesting at all [ev_economic_return_biaz12_21]. Region matters: the meta-analysis puts payback at 2 years for the average Asian farmer but more than 15 years for the average African farmer, at world maize prices [ev_economic_return_boum16_7]. In Mozambique basins did not differ significantly in net return from conventional tillage at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3], while in Ghana tied ridges with grass strips returned more than flat land in 2010 but not in 2011 [ev_economic_return_dalt14_3]. Farm size also matters: the Brazilian cistern income effect was confined to small farms and reversed on farms larger than 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5, ev_household_income_casag22_6]. Much of the literature comes from bundled programmes, lender reports and secondary citations, the Fox and meta-analysis returns are modelled, the Kenyan ridge-furrow net-income gains are from a single field trial, and the Tanzanian, Kenyan pond and stone-bund figures are cited in reviews [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_boum16_8, ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_biaz12_20]; the Indian pond returns are cross-sectional and confounded by farm size, and sand dams are judged likely not cost-efficient [ev_economic_return_pals23_1, ev_economic_return_ritc21_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty, and few studies follow households over time.

effect_mechanism: Household income and returns from mixed soil and water conservation and water-harvesting programmes have been found to rise, to stay flat and to fall. Gains run through higher yields, irrigation and diversification: a quasi-experimental study found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]; Brazil's production-cistern programme raised family income by about 4.6%, nearly 11% when the top of the income distribution is excluded, with larger effects on farms of 0 to 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_1, ev_household_income_casag22_2, ev_household_income_casag22_5]; a review of 311 Indian watershed case studies found a mean benefit-cost ratio of 2.14 and an internal rate of return of 22 percent [ev_economic_return_josh05_1, ev_economic_return_josh05_2]; Mauritanian dikes returned a financial IRR of 24% [ev_economic_return_mrt14_4]; and programme evaluations report income gains of 54% in Karnataka and 58% on the Loess Plateau over control areas [ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_iegchn07_6]. Losses come from costs exceeding gains: in Burkina Faso the yield increase did not cover the annual costs of single SWC measures [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3]; Ethiopian graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds had net present values of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4]; and the Brazilian cistern programme's benefit-cost ratio over its evaluation window was 0.0858 [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]. In Ethiopia, agricultural income from crops and livestock was significantly higher for users than non-users of micro- and macro-catchment techniques (cited in a review) [ev_household_income_biaz12_18], and in Tanzania investment in rainwater harvesting for maize, paddy rice and onion was profitable in the long term as long as farmers could afford the initial investment (Senkondo et al. 2004) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_19]. A meta-analysis valuing average maize gains at world prices puts payback of the water-harvesting investment at 4–5 years at the pooled-average gain, not accounting for capital interest [ev_economic_return_boum16_8]. On the loss side, stone rows and grass strips in Burkina Faso were not cost-effective without added nutrients because of high labour, transport and material costs (Zougmoré et al. 2004) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24].
conditionality: What separates the sides, where the evidence says it: farm size, since the Brazilian income effect was a gain on small farms but a loss on farms larger than 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5, ev_household_income_casag22_6]; labour costing and the size of the initial investment, since Ethiopian household benefit-cost ratios were 0.42 to 0.78 at market wages and exceeded one only with a shadow wage and a low initial investment [ev_economic_return_schmidt12_6]; and how long benefits are counted, since the Brazilian ratio covers a short window against a long-lived asset and counts income only [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]. For a Task Team Leader, the practical points are targeting smallholders, costing household labour honestly and expecting returns to arrive over years. The largest gains are from bundled programmes with weak attribution, and the Brazilian income effects are for a cistern bundled with a productive grant and training [ev_household_income_casag22_1]; IEG calls the China income estimate not robust and notes the India gains may partly be construction wages, and a Karnataka completion report doubts its own before/after figures [ev_household_income_iegchn07_6, ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_kar20_3]. The losses and nulls come mostly from independent evaluations, though the Ethiopian values may omit off-site benefits [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], and a Kenyan bundle showed no effect on per capita income [ev_household_income_mala24_2]. A review's report of increased incomes from check dams and infiltration pits in Malawi is qualitative and cited second-hand [ev_household_income_ngur26_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty. Location and up-front cost add to the separators: the same meta-analysis puts payback at 2 years for the average Asian farmer but more than 15 years for the average African farmer, whose average maize gain is far smaller [ev_economic_return_boum16_7], the Tanzanian profitability holds only where farmers can afford the initial investment [ev_economic_return_biaz12_19], and the Burkina Faso structures paid only with nutrients added [ev_economic_return_biaz12_24]. The payback periods are modelled from average yields, and the Ethiopian and Tanzanian findings are cited second-hand [ev_economic_return_boum16_8, ev_household_income_biaz12_18].

effect_mechanism: Zai pits, planting pits, contour bunds and planting basins can raise farm income by raising yields. effect_mechanism: Vallerani tractor-ploughed micro-catchments, half-moons and ridge-furrow systems collect runoff for crops and sown fodder. conditionality: The gains are per-hectare net incomes from field trials, not measured changes in household income or poverty, which they stand in for. effect_mechanism: Small reservoirs, sand dams, farm ponds, runoff cisterns and subsurface dams provide water for dry-season irrigation of vegetables and fruit and for livestock, shifting cropping towards higher-value crops and raising household income [ev_household_income_veno12_2, ev_household_income_ritc21_3]. In Kenya, farmers living near sand dams saw average income rise by 60% as more water in dry periods raised farm yields [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]. Reviews add that rainwater-harvesting ponds brought statistically significant gains in household income in Burkina Faso, water storage gave Ethiopian smallholders greater income security, harvested water used with precision irrigation in Ethiopia reached a net water value of up to 1.53 USD per cubic metre, and benefit-cost ratios reached up to 3.38 with payback periods of 6.8 to 12 years; Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_household_income_silv26_1, ev_household_income_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_silv26_1, ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. In Brazil, an Embrapa survey of some communities found small-farm incomes rose by about half a minimum wage per month after the second filling of the barraginhas [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. The Cambodian pond compiler rates farm income up because every crop yielded well once there was enough irrigation water [ev_household_income_wocat_2844_2017_farm_income]. Returns on stored runoff can be high: farm-pond supplemental irrigation of maize in Kenya gave net seasonal revenue of US$ 150 and could raise the annual return by 150% (Ngigi et al. 2005), road-catchment harvesting for paddy in Tanzania returned more than US$ 12 per person-day against US$ 3.7 for rainfed sorghum (Hatibu et al. 2006), and a Peruvian programme building 31 cochas returned 1.96 soles per sol invested (Tafur, cited in a programme review) [ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_biaz12_21, ev_economic_return_card22_1]. A Burkina Faso and Kenya model puts net profit from water harvesting with supplemental irrigation, fertiliser and an off-season tomato crop at 151–626 USD per hectare a year in Burkina Faso and 109–477 in Kenya, against at most 15 and 40–130 under current practice [ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_fox05_4]. In Pakistan, maize irrigated from harvested rainwater earned 0.28 US$ net per cubic metre in the first year, with a cumulative benefit-cost ratio projected at 2.02 by the second year and 3.53 by the third, and fish farming in a farm pond earned US$ 1799 net on average, about US$ 2951 in mini-dams [ev_economic_return_waqa25_5, ev_household_income_waqa25_7].
conditionality: Most literature magnitudes are secondary citations in reviews or vote counts [ev_household_income_saru19_3, ev_household_income_veno12_3]. Sand dams are judged likely not cost-efficient for water supply, Brazilian subsurface dams produced little cash income where electricity, investment capital or an irrigation tradition were missing, and the high Brazilian benefit-cost ratios come from an upper-middle-income context [ev_economic_return_ritc21_1, ev_household_income_cirilo03_7, ev_economic_return_cirilo03_10]. The Kenyan sand-dam income rise compares a small sample of households with a control catchment [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]; the reviewed figures are reported at their upper end, the Indian pond returns come from a cross-sectional survey confounded by farm size and assets [ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1], and the barraginha income finding is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology from an informal survey [ev_household_income_mira19_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty. The returns hinge on what the water is used for and on inputs: in the Burkina Faso model the yield gain from supplemental irrigation alone does not compensate for the labour and capital invested [ev_economic_return_fox05_2], and in Pakistan pearl millet irrigated from harvested rainwater lost 0.27 US$ per cubic metre in the first year and stayed below break-even by the third [ev_economic_return_waqa25_6]. The Kenyan, Tanzanian and Peruvian returns are second-hand citations, the model profits rely on a high-value tomato crop and vary with the cost put on labour, and the Pakistani figures are projections assuming constant prices and water productivity [ev_economic_return_biaz12_20, ev_economic_return_card22_1, ev_economic_return_fox05_3, ev_economic_return_waqa25_5].

effect_mechanism: Terracing raises yields and enables higher-value crops on former hillsides, which drives modelled returns per hectare above cost; terrace investments are judged to pay off over long lifetimes, mainly where they carry high-value crops such as vegetables [ev_economic_return_rwa18_8, ev_economic_return_willem21_1, ev_economic_return_fao13c_1]. WOCAT compilers report income from diverse crops behind contour stone bunds in Bhutan [ev_household_income_wocat_6891_2023_farm_income]. An Ethiopian synthesis reports net present values of 3486.2 Birr per hectare for stone bunds, 2794.0 for bench terraces and 5283.4 for level fanya juu [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_economic_return_adim16_3], and modelled bench-terrace gains in Peru could raise per capita incomes by up to 15% [ev_household_income_wei16_1]. A review cites soil and water conservation measures, including level bunds and fanya juu terraces, boosting farmer income by increasing soil fertility, yield and water [ev_household_income_tade23h1_1]. Field data from Ethiopia's Anjene catchment now measure the gain directly: teff, barley and maize grown on terraces earned an incremental income advantage of US$ 159, 275 and 141 per hectare per year over un-terraced farms, and at a 10% discount rate the average net present value of terrace investment for barley over 50 years was US$ 1542, and net present values were above zero across the catchment [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4, ev_economic_return_adgo13_5, ev_economic_return_adgo13_6, ev_economic_return_adgo13_10]. A review cites stone bunds giving a return rate of 50% in terms of farm profit (Gebremedhin et al., 1999) [ev_economic_return_gebr18_3].
conditionality: Several of the literature returns are lender crop-budget models for Rwanda and India [ev_economic_return_rwa18_8, ev_household_income_utk22_9]. Not every return is large: banquette profitability in Niger was of the order of 1% [ev_economic_return_heusch95_1]. The Ethiopian net present values are unweighted means from a small set of studies, the Peruvian income gain is a modelled potential cited in a review, and the Ethiopian income claim is cited from a study the citing review itself describes as methodologically weak [ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_household_income_wei16_1, ev_household_income_tade23h1_1]. Income and returns are proxies for poverty. The Anjene income figures exclude family labour and come from terraces that the community has maintained for decades, so they show what long-lived, maintained terraces return rather than the first years after building [ev_economic_return_adgo13_4]; the stone-bund return rate is cited second-hand [ev_economic_return_gebr18_3].

effect_mechanism: Terraces, stone bunds and lines, banquettes, trenches, pits and check dams slow overland flow and spread it behind barriers, so less runoff leaves the slope and less soil is detached and carried away; check dams and gabions trap sediment in channels. Measured reductions are large: terraces cut soil losses on small mountain plots from more than 200 to under 2 t/ha a year, Burundi terrace plots cut erosion by 50% to 90%, trenches reduced soil loss by 73.0% on average, and check dams cut catchment sediment export by 20 to 98% [ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_1_s, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_2_s, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_1, ev_sediment_retention_fran21_1]. WOCAT compilers across many countries rate soil loss, surface runoff and downstream siltation as reduced, explaining that micro-catchments cut the kinetic energy of rain by trapping runoff that check dams slow runoff so soil accumulates upstream, and that gabion walls and check dams trap sediment that would otherwise travel downstream [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_2895_2017_soil_loss, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_6716_2023_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_7778_2026_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_7778_2026_downstream_siltation]. Meta-analyses confirm the direction: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 58.66% and runoff by 53% on average, with soil-loss reductions of 68.67% for mulching, 54.97% for ridging, 55.06% for soil and stone bunds and 60.21% for terraces [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_1, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_1, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_3, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_4, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_5]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports soil loss down 59% under graded soil bunds, 88% under level soil bunds, 38% under stone bunds, 98% under mulch and 62% under tied ridging [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_3, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_4, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_5]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds erosion control on terraces 11.46 times that of controls and runoff reduction 2.6 times [ev_erosion_hazard_wei16_1, ev_runoff_reduction_wei16_1]. Reviews add further cited figures: Nyssen et al. (2007) found stone bunds cutting soil erosion by 68%, Gebremichael et al. (2005) recorded soil loss on cropland in Dogu'a Tembien falling from 57 to 20 t per hectare a year after physical conservation works, Lanckriet et al. (2012) measured 14.4 against 35.4 t per hectare a year under conservation agriculture compared with plain tillage, Al-Seekh and Mohammad (2009) found stone-terraced hillslopes reducing runoff by 65–85% and soil erosion by 58–69%, Araya and Stroosnijder (2010) found tied ridges cutting runoff by about 60%, Hulugalle (1990) recorded 0% to 15% of seasonal rainfall lost as runoff with tied ridging against 20–40% with open ridging or flat planting, and Lal (1982) found runoff and erosion 2.7 and 15.3 times higher in non-terraced than terraced catchments [ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_1, ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_13, ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_6, ev_runoff_reduction_stav20_1, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_7, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_11, ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_1]; a terracing review concludes that soil loss from cultivated slopes is much higher without terraces, which increase infiltration and interrupt hydrological connectivity [ev_erosion_hazard_arna15_4, ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_5]. At catchment scale, stone bunds, check dams and regrowth in Ethiopia cut sediment yield from 8.5 to 1.9 t per hectare a year, and check dams on China's Loess Plateau reduced erosion rates from more than 200 to 20–25 t per hectare a year [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1, ev_erosion_hazard_luca21_1]; there, a watershed model shows check dams reducing runoff by 12% and sediment by 11.7%, and studies cited by Shi et al. report check dams cutting sediment load by 51.9% in the Huangfuchuan catchment and rainy-season runoff by 15.5%–28.9% in the Yanhe watershed [ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_1, ev_sediment_retention_shi19_2, ev_sediment_retention_shi19_8, ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_6]. In Tigray, physical conservation works are cited as decreasing runoff by up to 88%, and integrated catchment management at May Zeg Zeg cut surface runoff volume by 81% [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8]; well-designed check dams reduce stream power and channel erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_11]. A meta-analysis of mulching finds runoff reduced by 47.4% and soil loss by 76.2% against controls, soil loss by 70.9% on cropland, and reductions of 45.9% and 75.1% at rainfall intensities above 90 mm/h [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_2, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_3, ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_5, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6]. In Brazil, barraginhas dispersed across farms capture runoff water, which Embrapa says prevents erosion, siltation and the carrying of pollutants [ev_runoff_reduction_mira19_4, ev_erosion_hazard_mira19_5].
conditionality: The WOCAT units are practitioner ratings, and several literature sources are lender self-reports with before/after designs, perception surveys or catchment numbers that barely changed: the Rwanda sediment drop from 54 to 2.6 tons/ha a year has no control, and Indian sediment yield moved only from 71.6 to 69.3 tons per ha per year [ev_erosion_hazard_rwa18_1_s, ev_erosion_hazard_utk22_3, ev_erosion_hazard_yem12_5]; runoff reduction and sediment retention enter as component proxies. Contrary findings: check dams can cause downstream channel incision, diversion banquettes increased gully and bank erosion in Niger, trenches raised sediment in the first years, Maghreb banquettes were often erased or unmaintained, and abandoned terraces increase erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_fran21_1, ev_erosion_hazard_heusch95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_4, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_2]. A rangeland review adds that, about 30 years after abandonment, many channel runoff-control structures in southern Arizona had failed and some accelerated headcut retreat and scouring, that collapsing stone terraces across dry channel beds in the Israeli Negev induced rill and gully erosion, and that Nyssen et al. (2007) suggest excessive removal of surface stones to build terraces led to a threefold increase in sheet and rill erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_12, ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_13, ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_3]. Most harm is tied to failed upkeep or poor construction rather than to working structures. Terraces also pass on part of what they catch: a review puts the delivery ratio at about 20%–30% for sediment and 50%–60% for runoff, and in extreme rainfall the sediment accumulated on terraces can reach the channel; one cited Chinese catchment estimate is only 25.04 against 28.97 t per hectare a year [ev_sediment_retention_arna15_6, ev_erosion_hazard_arna15_3]. A catchment-restoration meta-analysis in Ethiopia finds minimal effect of catchment treatment on runoff in drought-prone areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_3]. In Tunisia gullied area on banquette land grew by 12% between 1963 and 1973, poorly maintained banquettes in Algeria accelerate erosion, and Algerian banquettes had no influence on the sedimentation rate of the Oued Fodda dam [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_1, ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2, ev_sediment_retention_arab04_1]; and USA check dams had no significant effect on the runoff volume of major storms [ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_2]. Many of the added figures are citations within reviews rather than primary measurements, and the Loess Plateau watershed effect is modelled [ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_1, ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_1]. The meta-analyses pool unweighted study means and are dominated by plot-scale East African studies, so catchment-scale effects remain less certain [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei16_1]. The mulching meta-analysis pools land uses including post-fire forest and bare land; cropland and tree crops were less effective in reducing runoff, both below 40%, and the mulching benefits decreased with increasing rainfall intensity under heavy rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_4, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6]. The barraginha erosion statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measurement [ev_runoff_reduction_mira19_4, ev_erosion_hazard_mira19_5].

justification.mechanism: Terraces, stone bunds and lines, banquettes, trenches, pits and check dams slow overland flow and spread it behind barriers, so less runoff leaves the slope and less soil is detached and carried away; check dams and gabions trap sediment in channels. Measured reductions are large: terraces cut soil losses on small mountain plots from more than 200 to under 2 t/ha a year, Burundi terrace plots cut erosion by 50% to 90%, trenches reduced soil loss by 73.0% on average, and check dams cut catchment sediment export by 20 to 98% [ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_1_s, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_2_s, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_1, ev_sediment_retention_fran21_1]. WOCAT compilers across many countries rate soil loss, surface runoff and downstream siltation as reduced, explaining that micro-catchments cut the kinetic energy of rain by trapping runoff that check dams slow runoff so soil accumulates upstream, and that gabion walls and check dams trap sediment that would otherwise travel downstream [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_2895_2017_soil_loss, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_6716_2023_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_7778_2026_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_7778_2026_downstream_siltation]. Meta-analyses confirm the direction: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 58.66% and runoff by 53% on average, with soil-loss reductions of 68.67% for mulching, 54.97% for ridging, 55.06% for soil and stone bunds and 60.21% for terraces [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_1, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_1, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_3, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_4, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_5]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports soil loss down 59% under graded soil bunds, 88% under level soil bunds, 38% under stone bunds, 98% under mulch and 62% under tied ridging [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_3, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_4, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_5]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds erosion control on terraces 11.46 times that of controls and runoff reduction 2.6 times [ev_erosion_hazard_wei16_1, ev_runoff_reduction_wei16_1]. Reviews add further cited figures: Nyssen et al. (2007) found stone bunds cutting soil erosion by 68%, Gebremichael et al. (2005) recorded soil loss on cropland in Dogu'a Tembien falling from 57 to 20 t per hectare a year after physical conservation works, Lanckriet et al. (2012) measured 14.4 against 35.4 t per hectare a year under conservation agriculture compared with plain tillage, Al-Seekh and Mohammad (2009) found stone-terraced hillslopes reducing runoff by 65–85% and soil erosion by 58–69%, Araya and Stroosnijder (2010) found tied ridges cutting runoff by about 60%, Hulugalle (1990) recorded 0% to 15% of seasonal rainfall lost as runoff with tied ridging against 20–40% with open ridging or flat planting, and Lal (1982) found runoff and erosion 2.7 and 15.3 times higher in non-terraced than terraced catchments [ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_1, ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_13, ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_6, ev_runoff_reduction_stav20_1, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_7, ev_runoff_reduction_biaz12_11, ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_1]; a terracing review concludes that soil loss from cultivated slopes is much higher without terraces, which increase infiltration and interrupt hydrological connectivity [ev_erosion_hazard_arna15_4, ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_5]. At catchment scale, stone bunds, check dams and regrowth in Ethiopia cut sediment yield from 8.5 to 1.9 t per hectare a year, and check dams on China's Loess Plateau reduced erosion rates from more than 200 to 20–25 t per hectare a year [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1, ev_erosion_hazard_luca21_1]; there, a watershed model shows check dams reducing runoff by 12% and sediment by 11.7%, and studies cited by Shi et al. report check dams cutting sediment load by 51.9% in the Huangfuchuan catchment and rainy-season runoff by 15.5%–28.9% in the Yanhe watershed [ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_1, ev_sediment_retention_shi19_2, ev_sediment_retention_shi19_8, ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_6]. In Tigray, physical conservation works are cited as decreasing runoff by up to 88%, and integrated catchment management at May Zeg Zeg cut surface runoff volume by 81% [ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_7, ev_runoff_reduction_gebr18_8]; well-designed check dams reduce stream power and channel erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_11]. A meta-analysis of mulching finds runoff reduced by 47.4% and soil loss by 76.2% against controls, soil loss by 70.9% on cropland, and reductions of 45.9% and 75.1% at rainfall intensities above 90 mm/h [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_2, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_3, ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_5, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6]. In Brazil, barraginhas dispersed across farms capture runoff water, which Embrapa says prevents erosion, siltation and the carrying of pollutants [ev_runoff_reduction_mira19_4, ev_erosion_hazard_mira19_5].
justification.conditionality: The WOCAT units are practitioner ratings, and several literature sources are lender self-reports with before/after designs, perception surveys or catchment numbers that barely changed: the Rwanda sediment drop from 54 to 2.6 tons/ha a year has no control, and Indian sediment yield moved only from 71.6 to 69.3 tons per ha per year [ev_erosion_hazard_rwa18_1_s, ev_erosion_hazard_utk22_3, ev_erosion_hazard_yem12_5]; runoff reduction and sediment retention enter as component proxies. Contrary findings: check dams can cause downstream channel incision, diversion banquettes increased gully and bank erosion in Niger, trenches raised sediment in the first years, Maghreb banquettes were often erased or unmaintained, and abandoned terraces increase erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_fran21_1, ev_erosion_hazard_heusch95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_roose06_4, ev_erosion_hazard_willem21_2]. A rangeland review adds that, about 30 years after abandonment, many channel runoff-control structures in southern Arizona had failed and some accelerated headcut retreat and scouring, that collapsing stone terraces across dry channel beds in the Israeli Negev induced rill and gully erosion, and that Nyssen et al. (2007) suggest excessive removal of surface stones to build terraces led to a threefold increase in sheet and rill erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_12, ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_13, ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_3]. Most harm is tied to failed upkeep or poor construction rather than to working structures. Terraces also pass on part of what they catch: a review puts the delivery ratio at about 20%–30% for sediment and 50%–60% for runoff, and in extreme rainfall the sediment accumulated on terraces can reach the channel; one cited Chinese catchment estimate is only 25.04 against 28.97 t per hectare a year [ev_sediment_retention_arna15_6, ev_erosion_hazard_arna15_3]. A catchment-restoration meta-analysis in Ethiopia finds minimal effect of catchment treatment on runoff in drought-prone areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_3]. In Tunisia gullied area on banquette land grew by 12% between 1963 and 1973, poorly maintained banquettes in Algeria accelerate erosion, and Algerian banquettes had no influence on the sedimentation rate of the Oued Fodda dam [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_1, ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2, ev_sediment_retention_arab04_1]; and USA check dams had no significant effect on the runoff volume of major storms [ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_2]. Many of the added figures are citations within reviews rather than primary measurements, and the Loess Plateau watershed effect is modelled [ev_erosion_hazard_gebr18_1, ev_runoff_reduction_shi19_1]. The meta-analyses pool unweighted study means and are dominated by plot-scale East African studies, so catchment-scale effects remain less certain [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei16_1]. The mulching meta-analysis pools land uses including post-fire forest and bare land; cropland and tree crops were less effective in reducing runoff, both below 40%, and the mulching benefits decreased with increasing rainfall intensity under heavy rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_4, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6]. The barraginha erosion statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measurement [ev_runoff_reduction_mira19_4, ev_erosion_hazard_mira19_5].

effect_mechanism: In the Maghreb, contour structures have been reported both to hold runoff and to accelerate erosion. Staggered earth bunds (tabia) in Morocco store the runoff of all rains below 50 mm on the field [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. In Algeria, a poorly maintained banquette becomes a factor accelerating erosion, because the smallest unrepaired breach triggers a chain reaction through the whole network in torrential and prolonged rains [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2].
conditionality: Two conditions separate the sides in the sources. Maintenance: the acceleration is tied explicitly to unrepaired breaches in state-built banquettes [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2]. Storm size: the tabia hold runoff only up to rains of 50 mm, and in bigger storms the excess overtops them and gullies the whole slope [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. The actionable reading is to plan and fund upkeep and spillways, not only construction. Elsewhere banquettes simply did not stop gullying: gullied areas on Tunisian banquette land grew by 12% between 1963 and 1973, and over 1947-1968 Algerian banquettes had no influence on the sedimentation rate of the Oued Fodda dam [ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_1, ev_sediment_retention_arab04_1]. Neither side is measured on plots: the protective statement is from an expert manual and the harmful ones are secondary citations within a national evaluation, and the two concern different structures, tabia and banquettes [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1, ev_erosion_hazard_arab04_2].

effect_mechanism: In high-income settings check dams and ponds trap sediment: loose-rock check dams on semi-arid USA rangeland watersheds retained 48.4% and 82.4% of total sediment yield and produced a twofold decline in outlet sediment per unit of peak runoff, four field-edge ponds in southern Germany trapped 54-85% of incoming sediment over 8 years, and a typical Belgian pond had a long-term trapping efficiency of 68% [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1, ev_sediment_retention_poly14_2, ev_sediment_retention_meko14_2, ev_sediment_retention_meko14_3]. Bench terracing in a small USA watershed reduced runoff by 9% and sediment yield by 58% [ev_runoff_reduction_meko14_1]. In Spain, terrace maintenance slowed runoff for events with a return period shorter than 8–10 years, and terraces in general interrupt flows, shrinking the runoff-contributing area and peak discharges (Bellin et al. 2009, cited in a review) [ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_5].
conditionality: The studies found real effects in both directions, and what separates them is whether the structures hold and where erosion is measured. The gains are sediment trapped behind working dams, ponds and terraces; the harms are erosion triggered by the structures themselves or by their failure: channel incision was observed below 81% of surveyed check dams in a Spanish catchment through the clear-water effect [ev_erosion_hazard_fran21_1], about 30 years after channel runoff-control structures on semi-arid Arizona rangelands were abandoned a large share had failed and some accelerated headcut retreat and scouring (Nichols et al. 2018) [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_12], and in the Israeli Negev traditional stone terraces across dry channels proved highly vulnerable to collapse, their failure inducing rill and gully erosion, so they need frequent maintenance [ev_erosion_hazard_stav20_13]. For a Task Team Leader the separators are maintenance over decades and design for the channel below the structure. Even working check dams had no statistically significant effect on the runoff volume of major storms, reducing only the number of runoff events from small storms by 60%, and the twofold decline in outlet sediment was significant only at α = 0.2 [ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_2, ev_runoff_reduction_poly14_1, ev_sediment_retention_poly14_2]. Most units are secondary citations in reviews, and the high-income settings (rangeland, arable fields with ponds, Mediterranean terraces) differ from smallholder water harvesting [ev_sediment_retention_meko14_2, ev_runoff_reduction_arna15_5].
